aarons-rod-and-the-bronze-serpent-nehush.context_blurb:
The book of Numbers follows the Israelites through their wilderness years after the escape from Egypt, led by Moses and his older brother Aaron, who became Israel's first high priest. Two strange signs from those years gather around a staff and a bronze snake, and the second sign comes back to trouble a king of Judah centuries later.

The first story begins with jealousy. Tribe after tribe muttered that Aaron had no special claim to the priesthood, so God set Moses a test. Each tribal chief handed over his staff, one for every tribe of Israel, and Moses left all twelve overnight in the Tabernacle, the tent where Israel worshipped.

At dawn eleven staffs were still dead wood. Aaron's had come alive: in a single night it had sprouted buds, opened into blossom and set ripe almonds. The almond is the first tree to flower in that land each year, so the staff carried a sign of first fruits. Aaron's staff stood for the house of Levi, and the sign ended the quarrel: Israel's priests would come from the tribe of Levi and from no other.

The flowering staff became a treasure. The New Testament letter to the Hebrews places it inside the Ark of the Covenant, the gold-covered chest Israel carried through the desert, beside the golden pot of manna and the stone tablets of the covenant. Later Jewish tradition argued over whether those things sat inside the chest or next to it, but Hebrews puts all three within.

The second story comes further along the march. The people turned on God and Moses again, crying that they had been led out of Egypt only to perish in the desert. Numbers says God answered with fiery serpents, snakes whose bite probably burned like fire with venom, and many people died. When the people repented, Moses made a serpent of bronze and raised it on a pole, and anyone bitten who looked up at it lived.

Centuries passed, and the bronze serpent was still kept in Jerusalem, where worshippers had started burning incense to it as if it were a god. King Hezekiah of Judah smashed it and mocked the pieces with a name, Nehushtan, a pun on nehoshet, the Hebrew word for brass, as if to say the relic was nothing more than a lump of metal.

abraham-called-from-ur-to-canaan-and-the.context_blurb:
Genesis, the first book of the Bible, opens the story of Israel's founding family with Abram, an old man, together with Sarai his wife and Lot, his brother's son. Some four thousand years ago, the story says, God called Abram away from home to walk hundreds of miles toward a country no one in his family had seen, and a chain of promises, new names and strange visitors followed.

The family set out from Ur of the Chaldees, a mighty walled city beside a southern river in Mesopotamia, and paused at Haran on the road north before turning toward Canaan. When Abram reached Shechem in Canaan's hill country, God appeared to him under a great oak and promised the land to his children's children, and Abram marked the place by building an altar there to God.

Years went by. Abram grew rich, but he had no son, and a servant stood to inherit everything. One night God took him outside and pointed him at the sky: he was to count the stars of heaven if he could, because his descendants would be as many.

The promise became a covenant, and the covenant brought new names. God renamed Abram as Abraham, meaning father of a multitude, and on that same day renamed his wife too: Sarai became Sarah.

Then came the visitors. Abraham was resting at his tent door in the noon heat, among the oaks of Mamre, when three strangers arrived, and he hurried to feed them with a calf and fresh cakes. One of them said that within a year Sarah would have a son. Sarah, overhearing from inside the tent, laughed to herself at the thought of a baby at her age, so when the boy came he was named Isaac, which means "he laughs".

Abraham's story holds an even stranger meeting. Years earlier Abram had rescued Lot from four raiding kings, and on his way home he was met by Melchizedek, both king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who brought out bread and wine and blessed him. His name means "king of righteousness", and Jewish and Christian writers have argued about him ever since.

The three visitors went on toward Sodom, and the cities of the plain burned under fire and brimstone. The angels told Lot and his family to run and not look back. Lot's wife turned for one last look at the home she was leaving and became a pillar of salt. Travellers later pointed to salt formations near the Dead Sea as what remained of her.

the-binding-of-isaac-on-mount-moriah.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, God tests the old patriarch Abraham by commanding him to take his son — the long-awaited child of promise he had waited decades for — up a mountain in the land of Moriah and offer him there as a burnt sacrifice. Abraham rises early, saddles his donkey, cuts the wood for the fire, and walks three days with the boy and two young servants. The moment the angel calls down from heaven at the last second echoes through the New Testament and the Quran. Source: Genesis 22 KJV.

jacobs-ladder-at-bethel-and-the-wrestlin.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, Isaac's younger son is a schemer. He first cheats his elder twin out of the firstborn's blessing by bringing their old blind father a cooked meal under a disguise. Fleeing his brother's rage, he lies down in the desert with a stone for a pillow and dreams of a stairway reaching from earth to heaven with angels moving up and down it. Years later, coming home with wives and children, he spends a whole night by a small river wrestling a mysterious stranger. He walks away with a limp, a new name, and the identity his descendants will carry forever. Sources: Genesis 25–32 KJV.

josephs-coat-of-many-colors-and-the-pit-.context_blurb: Jacob loved his son Joseph more than any of his other children because Joseph was the son of his old age, born late in life to his beloved wife Rachel. To mark him as the favored son Jacob gave him a striking garment the elder brothers hated him for. Joseph then made it worse by telling his family the dreams he kept having — dreams of sheaves and stars bowing down to him. The ten older brothers finally caught him alone in a pasture at Dothan and threw him into a dry pit while they argued what to do with him. Source: Genesis 37 KJV.

joseph-reveals-himself-i-am-joseph-your-.context_blurb: Years after being sold into slavery, Joseph has risen to the highest post in Egypt beneath Pharaoh. Famine has reached Canaan, and Jacob sends ten of his sons south to buy grain. They bow before the Egyptian vizier they do not recognize — the brother they threw into a pit more than twenty years before. Joseph puts them through a series of hard tests before the moment of recognition that is one of the great reunion scenes in the Hebrew Bible. Source: Genesis 42–45 KJV.

moses-in-the-basket-of-bulrushes.context_blurb: A new Pharaoh has arisen in Egypt who did not know Joseph. He enslaves the Hebrews and orders a horror against every newborn Hebrew boy. A Levite woman gives birth to a healthy son and hides him for as long as she can — then floats him down the Nile in a waterproofed basket of reeds, with the baby's older sister watching from the bank. The scene opens the whole Exodus story. Source: Exodus 1–2 KJV.

the-burning-bush-and-the-name-i-am.context_blurb: Years after fleeing Egypt as a young man, Moses has become a shepherd in Midian, tending the flock of his father-in-law. He leads the sheep to the backside of the desert and comes to the mountain of God, where he sees a bush that is on fire but is not being burned up. The voice that speaks from the bush gives him both his life's work and the great mysterious name of God that the Hebrew Bible treats as holiest of all. Source: Exodus 3–4 KJV.

the-ten-plagues-of-egypt.context_blurb: The book of Exodus tells how Moses and his brother Aaron go before Pharaoh and demand that the Hebrews be let out of Egypt. Each refusal brings a plague — ten in all, each worse than the last — that batter the land, the water, the livestock, and finally the firstborn of Egypt. Pharaoh breaks and lets them go, and the Hebrews march out carrying unleavened bread and bitter herbs for a Passover meal that would be kept once a year ever after. Source: Exodus 5–12 KJV.

the-parting-of-the-red-sea.context_blurb: The Hebrews have marched out of Egypt and are camped at the edge of the Red Sea when Pharaoh changes his mind one last time and sends his chariots after them. Moses stretches out his hand with his staff; God sends a wind that blows all night; the waters stand up on both sides and the Hebrews walk through on dry ground. When the Egyptian chariots follow in after them, the walls of water come back down. Source: Exodus 14 KJV.

sinai-the-tablets-and-the-golden-calf.context_blurb: Three months out of Egypt, the Hebrews reach the foot of a mountain in the Sinai wilderness. Thunder, cloud, and the long blast of a trumpet come down on it. Moses climbs up alone and stays forty days and forty nights. He comes down carrying two stone tablets inscribed by the finger of God — and finds that in his absence, Aaron and the people have made themselves a different god of molten gold. Source: Exodus 19–32 KJV.

noah-and-the-ark-the-raven-the-dove-and-.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, God sees that the whole human race has grown wicked and resolves to wipe it from the earth with a great flood. He chooses one man — Noah — and tells him to build a wooden ark, and to bring his family and pairs of every kind of animal onto it. Rain falls, the fountains of the deep break open, the ark floats, and when the waters finally begin to go down Noah sends out two different birds in turn to see whether dry land has come back. Source: Genesis 6–9 KJV.

hagar-and-ishmael-sent-into-the-wilderne.context_blurb: In the book of Genesis, Sarah has waited years for a child of her own and still has none. She hands her Egyptian handmaid Hagar to Abraham as a second wife so that he may have a son. Hagar bears him his first son, and years later — after Sarah bears a son of her own in old age, as the story tells it — the family fractures. Sarah demands that Hagar and the boy be sent away; Abraham sends them off with a loaf and a bottle of water. Alone in the wilderness of Beersheba, the water runs out. Source: Genesis 16, 21 KJV.

deborah-barak-sisera-and-jaels-tent-peg.context_blurb:
In the age of the Judges, before Israel had kings, a prophetess named Deborah led the people. The book of Judges tells her story twice, once in prose and once in an ancient victory song, and it ends with a general killed not by a warrior but by a woman with a tent peg.

Deborah judged Israel sitting under a palm tree in the hill country of Ephraim, between Ramah and Bethel, and people called it the palm of Deborah.

Israel was groaning under Jabin, the Canaanite king who ruled from Hazor, and his general Sisera, so Deborah called the war-captain Barak and gave him God's command to raise ten thousand men and go to war. Barak would go only if Deborah went with him. She agreed, but warned him that the glory of the day would go to a woman.

Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots, and for twenty years he had used them to grind Israel down; iron was still rare and costly then, and Israel's foot soldiers had nothing that could face them on open ground. Barak mustered on Mount Tabor, and Sisera's chariots rolled down into the valley of the river Kishon. A sudden storm turned the riverbed to mud, the heavy wheels stuck fast, and Sisera's army broke and ran.

Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite. She welcomed him in, hid him under a mantle, and when he asked for water she gave him milk instead, butter in a lordly dish as the song remembers it. Warm and full, he fell into an exhausted sleep. Then Jael took up a hammer and a tent peg, crept to him and drove the peg through his temple. Deborah's warning to Barak had come true.

Deborah's victory song in Judges 5 refuses to give all the credit to spears or to a tent peg. It says heaven itself fought: the stars fought from their courses against Sisera, and the river Kishon swept his army away.

Its last verses leave the battle behind for a Canaanite palace, with Sisera's mother at a latticed window, peering down the road and asking why his chariot was so slow to come home, while her ladies assured her the men must be sharing out the spoils. The listener knows that her son lies dead in Jael's tent.

gideon-the-fleece-the-three-hundred-and-.context_blurb: In the book of Judges, the Midianites' camel-raids have driven Israel into caves. An angel finds Gideon of Ophrah hiding to beat out his wheat in an unexpected place and greets him as 'thou mighty man of valour.' Gideon asks for sign after sign to be sure the call is real, then whittles his army down from thirty-two thousand men to a famous small number for the night raid on the Midianite camp. Source: Judges 6–7 KJV.

samson-the-honey-in-the-lion-the-jawbone.context_blurb: In the book of Judges, an angel visits the barren wife of Manoah of Zorah and tells her the son she will bear must be a Nazarite from the womb — sworn to God his whole life, forbidden ever to let a razor touch his head. He grows up to be the strongest and strangest of Israel's judges, a one-man wrecking crew against the Philistines who makes riddles, tears a lion apart with his bare hands, and finally brings down a pagan temple on his own head. Source: Judges 13–16 KJV.

ruth-gleaning-in-the-field-of-boaz.context_blurb: The book of Ruth opens in the days of the Judges, when a famine drives a Bethlehemite named Elimelech to leave Israel with his wife Naomi and their two sons. The family settles in a neighboring country east of the Dead Sea, where the sons both marry local women. When all three men die, Naomi walks home empty-handed; one of her foreign daughters-in-law refuses to be sent away and walks beside her. The rest of the book is about how that foreign widow is gathered into Israel in a barley-field at Bethlehem. Source: Ruth KJV.

joshua-at-jericho-the-trumpets-and-the-w.context_blurb: After Moses dies on Mount Nebo in sight of the Promised Land but never entering it, one man takes his place and leads Israel across the Jordan on dry ground. Their first target is Jericho, a walled city sitting on the plain. Before the attack two spies slip inside, find shelter in a surprising house, and promise its mistress a sign of safety for her family when the city falls. Source: Joshua 2–6 KJV.

the-defeat-at-ai-and-joshuas-long-day.context_blurb: Fresh from the fall of Jericho, Joshua expects an easy second win against the small nearby city of Ai. The Israelite force is routed, and the question is why. The problem turns out to be a man named Achan, who had taken plunder from Jericho that was supposed to belong to God alone. Later in the same campaign, Joshua is caught in a long day of fighting against five southern kings and prays for the sun and moon to stand still until the battle is finished. Source: Joshua 7, 10 KJV.

choose-you-this-day-whom-ye-shall-serve-.context_blurb:
Joshua succeeded Moses as the leader of Israel, took the people across the Jordan and led the conquest of Canaan in the book that bears his name. In its last chapter he is an old man, and he gathers the tribes for a farewell that gave the world a line still quoted everywhere.

Joshua told the assembled tribes to choose that very day whom they would serve, and he ended with the words that have travelled around the world: whatever the rest of them chose, he and his house would serve the God of Israel.

He held the farewell at Shechem, in the hills of Ephraim, the old covenant town where long before Abraham had pitched his tent and built his first altar in Canaan, and where Jacob had paid a hundred silver pieces for a field.

The old warrior had seen wonders. Years earlier he had led the march around Jericho, with seven priests carrying trumpets of rams' horn before the Ark. For six days the people circled the city once a day, and on the seventh day they went around it seven times; then the trumpets sounded, the people shouted, and the wall fell down flat.

The book ends with two burials. Joshua was laid in his grave, and so at last were the bones of Joseph, brought up from Egypt by his people and carried all through the wilderness years; they buried them at Shechem, in the field Jacob had bought.

david-and-goliath.context_blurb:
The duel of David and Goliath in 1 Samuel 17 is the most famous underdog story in the Western world. A shepherd boy with a sling faces a giant champion in bronze armour, and the story is full of small, exact details that make it come alive.

The Philistines and King Saul's Israelites were camped on two hills, with the Valley of Elah lying between them. Twice a day, at dawn and at dusk, the Philistine giant Goliath came striding down in his bronze armour and challenged the Israelites to send out one man to fight him, and for forty days not one of them went down to meet him.

David was not with the army. His father Jesse sent him from the sheepfold with food for his three eldest brothers, an ephah of parched grain and ten loaves of bread, and ten cheeses for their captain.

When David offered to fight, Saul dressed him in the king's own armour, but David took it off. Instead he went to the brook, picked five smooth stones out of the water, and dropped them into his shepherd's bag.

Goliath cursed him, and David answered that the giant came with sword and spear and shield, but that he himself came in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel's armies, so that all the earth would know there was a God in Israel. David ran at him, slung one stone, and it sank into Goliath's forehead, and the giant fell on his face to the earth. Scholars still puzzle over how a helmeted giant left his brow exposed.

The story has a dark sequel. Years later, fleeing King Saul, David came unarmed to the priest Ahimelech at the sanctuary town of Nob, and the priest fed him with the holy bread and gave him Goliath's own sword. For that kindness Saul ordered Doeg the Edomite to cut down Ahimelech along with eighty-five priests of the town.

A puzzle hides in the text as well. At 2 Samuel 21:19 the credit for killing Goliath of Gath goes to another man of Bethlehem, Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim. The parallel verse in 1 Chronicles smooths it over by saying that Elhanan killed Lahmi, Goliath's brother.

david-and-jonathan-the-sworn-brotherhood.context_blurb:
Jonathan was the eldest son of King Saul of Israel and heir to the throne. From the day the young David killed Goliath, the books of Samuel say, Jonathan loved him as his own soul, and their sworn brotherhood held even when Saul tried to kill David, and even though David was marked to take the crown Jonathan should have worn.

Jonathan sealed the friendship by stripping off his own royal robe and his garments and giving them to David, together with his sword, his bow and his belt: the outward signs of a prince handed to the man who would one day take his place.

Saul grew jealous of David's fame. Twice, while David played the harp to soothe the king's black moods, Saul seized his javelin and flung it at him, meaning to pin him to the wall, and twice David slipped aside.

David fled and hid in a field, and Jonathan arranged a signal. He would come out as if for archery practice and shoot three arrows past a servant boy: if he shouted that the arrows lay on this side, David was safe, and if he shouted that they lay beyond, David must run. The arrows went beyond. The two friends met in secret one last time, wept on each other's necks, and swore an oath that God would stand between them, and between my seed and thy seed forever: their children, and their children's children. Years later that oath saved Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth.

Then the Philistines broke Israel's army on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan and his brothers were cut down around their father, and Saul, wounded by archers, fell on his own sword when his armour-bearer would not kill him. The Philistines hung the bodies on the wall of Beth-shan, but the men of Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul had once saved from the Ammonites, marched through the night, took the bodies down, burned them beneath a tamarisk tree at home and fasted seven days.

When the news reached David, he sang a lament over Saul and Jonathan whose refrain still echoes: How are the mighty fallen. Turning to Jonathan alone, he called him my brother and said that Jonathan's love for him had been wonderful, passing the love of women.

david-and-bathsheba-and-nathan-the-proph.context_blurb:
King David is the great hero-king of the Hebrew Bible, the shepherd boy who killed Goliath. But the Second Book of Samuel does not hide his darkest hour: the story of Bathsheba, a husband sent to his death, and a prophet brave enough to tell the king to his face what he had done.

It begins in spring, the season when kings rode out to war. David's general Joab was besieging Rabbah, the Ammonite capital across the Jordan, but David had stayed at home in Jerusalem, in his own palace. One evening he rose from his bed and strolled across the palace rooftop, and from there he saw a very beautiful woman bathing in a courtyard below.

Her name was Bathsheba, and she was the wife of Uriah the Hittite, a foreigner who fought for Israel and was later named among David's thirty mighty men. David took her for himself, and when she was expecting his child he arranged for Uriah to be killed in battle and married the widow.

Then the prophet Nathan came to the king with a story. A rich man with great flocks and herds had a poor neighbour who owned only one little ewe lamb, which he had brought up indoors, sharing his food and his cup with it and holding it like a daughter. When a traveller came to visit, the rich man spared his own flock and took the poor man's lamb for the meal.

David burned with anger and swore that such a man deserved to die. Nathan answered him in four words: Thou art the man. The lamb was Bathsheba, and the rich man was the king.

Bathsheba's baby fell sick. For seven days David fasted and lay on the ground, refusing food. When the child died, his servants were afraid to tell him, but David got up, washed, put on fresh clothes and asked for a meal. He told them that while the child lived there had been hope; now he would one day go to the child, but the child would never come back to him.

elijahs-mantle-and-the-harp-of-david-the.context_blurb:
The Hebrew Bible is full of remembered objects that carry a person's whole story: a shepherd's harp, a prophet's cloak, a pair of bronze pillars, a staff that flowers. Each one marks a calling, a succession or a choice.

When an evil spirit tormented King Saul and drove him to rage, the young shepherd David of Bethlehem was brought to play for him, and whenever David played the harp the king was refreshed and the spirit left him. The Hebrew word, kinnor, really means a small lyre, but harp is the word the story is remembered by.

When Elijah's time was nearly over, he found his successor, Elisha son of Shaphat, ploughing behind twelve pairs of oxen, and without a word he threw his mantle across Elisha's shoulders. Elisha would take up that same mantle again at the Jordan when Elijah was gone.

Only one verse describes Elijah's own look: a hairy man with a girdle of leather about his waist, so distinctive that a king knew him from the description alone. Centuries later John the Baptist came out of the wilderness wearing camel's hair and the same leather belt, and people wondered whether Elijah had come back.

When Solomon built the Temple in Jerusalem, he set two huge bronze pillars before its porch and gave each a name: on the right Jachin, meaning he shall establish, and on the left Boaz, meaning in him is strength.

Some of these objects seem alive. When the tribes of Israel quarrelled over the priesthood, a rod for each tribe was laid overnight before the Ark, and by morning Aaron's rod had budded, blossomed and borne ripe almonds, marking his tribe of Levi as Israel's priests.

elijah-at-cherith-and-zarephath-the-rave.context_blurb:
Elijah the Tishbite is the fiercest prophet of the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Kings 17 he confronts King Ahab of Israel with an oath: no dew and no rain until he says so. Then he has to vanish, because the king and his queen want him dead.

The queen hunting him was Jezebel, Ahab's foreign-born wife, daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, who was killing the prophets of Israel's God wherever she found them. God sent Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan, and there ravens brought him bread and meat every morning and every evening, unclean birds keeping the prophet alive, while he drank from the brook.

When the brook dried up, God sent him to a widow in Zarephath, a town on the coast of Sidon, deep in the very land Jezebel came from, where no hunter of hers would search.

At the town gate he found the widow gathering firewood and asked her for water and a little bread. She told him she had nothing baked, only a handful of flour and the last of her oil, and that she was gathering two sticks to bake a last small cake so that she and her boy could eat one last time and then die. Elijah told her to bake for him first, and promised that her barrel of meal would not run out, nor her cruse of oil fail, until the rain returned; and so it was.

Later the widow's son fell sick and stopped breathing. Elijah carried the boy up to his own room, laid him on his bed, lay down full length upon the child three times, calling on God, and the child's breath came back. He carried the boy down to his mother with four words: See, thy son liveth.

Not everyone at Ahab's court served Jezebel. The king's own steward, Obadiah, who secretly feared God, hid a hundred prophets in caves, fifty to a cave, and fed them on bread and water.

The New Testament remembers the drought twice, in Luke, where Jesus recalls Israel's many widows, and in the letter of James, which praises Elijah's prayer, and both give it the same length: three and a half years.

mount-carmel-elijah-and-the-prophets-of-.context_blurb: After three years of drought, the prophet Elijah challenges King Ahab's four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal to a showdown on the top of Mount Carmel. Each side builds an altar, lays a bull on it, and calls on its god to answer by fire. Elijah pours water three times over his altar until a trench around the stones is full before he even prays. Source: 1 Kings 18 KJV.

horeb-the-still-small-voice-the-fiery-ch.context_blurb: Hours after fire fell on his sacrifice at Carmel, the prophet Elijah learns that Queen Jezebel has sworn by her gods to have him killed by the next day. He runs for his life a day's journey into the wilderness and sits down under a lonely tree to die. Instead he is fed by an angel, walks forty days and forty nights to the mountain where Moses once met God, and hears the Lord in an unexpected form — not in wind, earthquake, or fire. The chapter closes with his final journey and the strange way he leaves this world. Source: 1 Kings 19; 2 Kings 2 KJV.

elisha-the-double-portion-the-bears-and-.context_blurb: The young farmer Elisha has just been called from his father's plow by the old prophet Elijah. To show he is not going back, he kills his own oxen and gives his village a farewell feast — burning the equipment of his old life as the cooking-fire. The rest of 2 Kings is a sequence of his famous miracles: a floating iron axe-head, a Syrian commander's cure, a dead boy raised by lying on him and sneezing seven times, and even one strange story that keeps working after Elisha himself is already dead and buried. Source: 2 Kings 2–13 KJV.

jonah-the-great-fish-nineveh-and-the-gou.context_blurb: The Hebrew Bible book of Jonah tells how God sent a reluctant prophet east to call the wicked Assyrian capital of Nineveh to repent. Jonah does not want to go. He goes down to the Mediterranean port of Joppa, pays his fare, and boards a ship sailing the opposite way, toward far Tarshish. The great storm, the lots, the swallow by a great fish, the second call, and the quarrel at the end over a gourd-vine are all in the book's four short chapters. Source: Jonah 1–4 KJV.

daniel-in-the-lions-den.context_blurb:
The Book of Daniel follows a young Jewish captive who rises to power in the courts of foreign kings. Its most famous story comes in chapter 6, when the old statesman's rivals turn the law against him and he spends a night shut in with hungry beasts.

When King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon took Jerusalem, he carried off the brightest young Hebrew captives to train at his court, and Daniel was among them. The Babylonians renamed the boys after their own gods, and Daniel became Belteshazzar.

Decades later, under King Darius the Mede, Daniel was a great official, and jealous rivals persuaded Darius to sign a law forbidding prayer to any god or man except Darius for the next thirty days, on pain of death. Daniel did not hide. He climbed to the upper room of his house and, as he always did, knelt three times a day by windows open toward Jerusalem, the city of the Temple, toward which the exiles turned to pray. So Darius, trapped by his own law, had him thrown into a den of lions.

The den's mouth was blocked with a great stone, and Darius sealed it with his own signet ring and the rings of his lords, so that no one, not even the king, could change what had been done to Daniel.

Darius spent a sleepless night without food, and at first light he ran to the den and called down to Daniel. Daniel answered from the dark that his God had sent an angel who shut the lions' mouths, so that they had not harmed him. Daniel was drawn up without a scratch, and Darius turned his fury on the men who had tricked him: he had them thrown into the den along with their wives and children, and the lions overpowered them before they reached the bottom.

belshazzars-feast-and-the-writing-on-the.context_blurb:
The Book of Daniel, in the Hebrew Bible, tells of the last night of Babylon's power. Around 539 BC the Persian armies of Cyrus were closing in on the great city, yet inside the palace the king was throwing a banquet. Chapter 5 tells what happened when a hand came out of the air and began to write on his wall.

The king was Belshazzar, and his feast was a wild one, with a thousand of his lords drinking in the hall. Halfway through, he sent for the gold and silver cups that Nebuchadnezzar, the king Daniel calls his father, had carried off long before from the Temple in Jerusalem when his army sacked the city. The guests drank from the holy vessels and praised their own gods, and the writer of Daniel does not even name those gods. He simply lists what the idols were made of: gold and silver, brass and iron, wood and stone.

In that same hour, close to the great lampstand, fingers appeared, a man's hand with no arm or body, and began writing across the plastered wall of the palace.

None of the king's astrologers could read the words. Then the queen-mother remembered Daniel, a captive from Judah who had served in Nebuchadnezzar's day. Belshazzar promised him three things if he could read the writing: a robe of scarlet, a chain of gold for his neck, and the rank of third ruler in the kingdom. Third, because Belshazzar himself ruled as second, under his father Nabonidus, a detail archaeologists later confirmed.

Daniel turned down the gifts and read out the four Aramaic words on the wall: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. Then he explained them to the king's face, and the middle word, tekel, carried the line still quoted at any moment of reckoning: Belshazzar had been weighed in the balances and found wanting.

Daniel had told the king his kingdom was finished, and the very next verse is brutally short: that same night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was killed. Darius the Mede, a man of about sixty-two, took the kingdom after him.

nebuchadnezzars-dream-and-the-fiery-furn.context_blurb: King Nebuchadnezzar, the mightiest ruler of the ancient world, has torn Daniel and his three Jewish friends out of Judah and marched them east into captivity. The king first dreams a great statue made of several different metals in layers, and only Daniel can tell him both the dream and its meaning. Later the king sets up a huge golden image on the plain of Dura, orders every subject to bow when the music plays, and when Daniel's three friends refuse he throws them into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. Source: Daniel 2–3 KJV.

esther-mordecai-haman-and-the-feast-of-p.context_blurb: The Hebrew Bible book of Esther is set in the Persian capital of Shushan under King Ahasuerus. Queen Vashti is deposed for refusing to be paraded before the drunken Persian lords, and a beauty search across the empire turns up a young Jewish orphan named Hadassah, raised by her cousin Mordecai. She is brought to the palace and crowned queen under a Persian name. Then a vizier named Haman proposes to kill every Jew in the empire — and Queen Esther has to risk her neck to speak for her people. Source: Esther 1–10 KJV.

isaiah-coals-to-the-lips-and-the-seraphi.context_blurb: In the sixth chapter of the Hebrew Bible book of Isaiah, a young prophet in Jerusalem stands in the Temple in the year King Uzziah dies and sees the Lord sitting upon a throne 'high and lifted up.' The hem of the robe alone fills the whole Temple. Six-winged burning ones hover above the throne crying 'Holy, holy, holy.' The prophet cries out that he is undone, a man of unclean lips — and one of the burning ones flies to him with a coal from the altar. Source: Isaiah 6 KJV.

jeremiah-the-potters-wheel-and-the-linen.context_blurb: In the days of King Josiah of Judah, the Lord calls a young priest's son of Jerusalem to be the prophet to a kingdom staggering toward destruction by Babylon. His call-scene, his tour of a working potter's shop, his object-lessons with a hidden linen belt and a smashed earthen jar, his imprisonment at the hands of his own countrymen, and the Ethiopian servant who hauls him up out of a mud-pit by old rags under the arms are all in the book that carries his name. Source: Jeremiah 1–38 KJV.

ezekiel-the-wheel-and-the-valley-of-dry-.context_blurb: By the river Chebar in Babylon, a young exile priest sees the heavens open in his thirtieth year — a cloud from the north with fire enfolding itself and brightness round about it. He becomes the strangest visionary in the Hebrew Bible. His wheels within wheels, his vision of a valley of dry bones that come back together bone to bone, his siege-models and his lying on his side for forty days are all gathered in the book that bears his name. Source: Ezekiel 1, 37 KJV.

samuel-anointing-saul-and-later-david.context_blurb: Before he was ever born, the prophet Samuel was promised to God by a barren mother who had wept and prayed at the shrine of Shiloh until the priest Eli mistook her silent moving lips for drunkenness. Samuel grew up to be the last of the judges of Israel and the kingmaker who anointed its first two kings — first a tall Benjaminite who hid among the baggage out of embarrassment, and then, long after the first king had been rejected, a young shepherd summoned in from the pasture by Samuel at Jesse's house in Bethlehem. Sources: 1 Samuel 1, 10, 16 KJV.

solomon-wisdom-the-two-mothers-the-templ.context_blurb: In 1 Kings of the Hebrew Bible, the young king Solomon — son of David by Bathsheba — goes up to the high place at Gibeon to offer sacrifice. That night God appears to him in a dream with a startling offer: 'Ask what I shall give thee.' Instead of long life or riches, Solomon asks for one thing, and his wisdom becomes famous across the ancient world. The two mothers before his throne, the building of the Temple in Jerusalem, and the visit of the Queen of Sheba all follow from that early choice. Source: 1 Kings 3–10 KJV.

solomons-temple-menorah-showbread-and-th.context_blurb: In 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, King Solomon builds in Jerusalem the first great Temple of God in Israel. For seven years and more he gathers cedar from Lebanon, hammered gold, olivewood for the giant inner cherubim, and twelve brazen oxen to carry the molten sea. The Holy Place has a seven-lamped golden lampstand, a table of showbread, and ten lavers for washing; and the inmost chamber shelters the Ark of the Covenant with the tablets from Mount Horeb. Sources: 1 Kings 6–8; 2 Chronicles 3–7 KJV.

bethlehem-the-manger-and-the-shepherds.context_blurb:
The Gospel of Luke tells the best-known birth story in the Western world. Joseph and Mary journey from Nazareth to Bethlehem, in the hill country of Judea, and there Mary's son Jesus is born in the humblest possible place, while out in the fields the first visitors hear the news.

They travel because the emperor Caesar Augustus has ordered a census of the whole empire, and each man must be counted in his family's home town; Joseph's is Bethlehem. There Mary wraps her newborn son in swaddling clothes and lays him in a manger, a trough that animals eat from; the word itself comes from a Latin root meaning to eat. Luke gives the reason in a blunt half-line: the inn had no room for them. Luke never mentions an ox or a donkey; later artists borrowed those from the prophet Isaiah.

On the hillside outside town, shepherds were keeping watch over their flocks by night when an angel appeared, and Luke says the glory of the Lord shone round about them, and they were terrified.

Then the sky filled with angels. Their song opens with glory to God in the highest, and its second half promises peace on earth and good will toward men. The shepherds ran into Bethlehem, found the couple and the child in his manger, and told everyone what the angel had said. Then Luke turns to Mary by herself: she kept all these things, turning them over quietly and pondering them in her heart.

Twelve centuries later, at Christmas 1223, Francis of Assisi brought Luke's scene to life. In a hillside cave at Greccio, a small hill town north of Rome, his friend Giovanni Velita set up a real manger full of hay, with an ox and a donkey standing by, villagers came with torches and candles, and Mass was said over the crib: the first live nativity scene.

gabriel-to-mary-and-the-leap-in-elizabet.context_blurb: In the first chapter of the Gospel of Luke, an angel appears to a young woman named Mary in a house in Nazareth in Galilee. He greets her with 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured' and tells her she will bear a son called Jesus. Mary asks a single startled question in reply. The scene then crosses the hill country of Judea to the house of Mary's older kinswoman Elizabeth, whose own long-barren pregnancy with the future John the Baptist has already made the elderly priest Zacharias mute. Source: Luke 1 KJV.

the-magi-the-star-herod-and-the-flight-t.context_blurb: Matthew's Gospel opens its Nativity story with strangers walking into Jerusalem from a long way east. They go straight to the palace of King Herod the Great and ask the question that terrifies him — where is the newborn king of the Jews? They explain how they knew to come at all. Herod sends them on to Bethlehem with orders to come back and tell him what they find; instead they go home another way, and the holy family flees south to escape what Herod does next. Source: Matthew 2 KJV.

the-boy-jesus-in-the-temple-at-twelve.context_blurb: Only one of the four Gospels gives any scene from Jesus's childhood after the Nativity itself. Luke tells how his parents went every year to a great feast in Jerusalem, and the one year they lost him on the trip home. They turn back and look for a day and a half, and finally find him in the Temple — sitting among the teachers of the Law. The scene closes with the first words of Jesus the gospels record. Source: Luke 2:41–52 KJV.

john-the-baptist-locusts-honey-and-the-d.context_blurb: Out in the desert country east of Jerusalem, a wild preacher stands by the river and calls the crowds to turn their lives around. He dresses like the old Hebrew prophets — a rough coat and a leather belt — and eats whatever the wilderness provides. He is the long-promised son of the old priest Zacharias and his wife, named by an angel at Zacharias's altar of incense. One day his young kinsman Jesus walks down out of Galilee to be baptised by him in the river, and a voice from heaven speaks over the water. The baptizer later loses his head at Herod's birthday banquet in Machaerus. Source: Matthew 3, 14; Luke 1 KJV.

forty-days-in-the-wilderness-the-three-t.context_blurb: Right after his baptism in the Jordan, Jesus goes out alone into the wilderness. He eats nothing for a set stretch of time that Matthew and Luke both give the same figure for. The devil then meets him there, and tests him three times — one test with hunger, one with power, and one with a leap from a dizzying height. Each test ends with Jesus answering by quoting a line of Deuteronomy from memory. Source: Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13 KJV.

water-into-wine-at-the-wedding-in-cana.context_blurb: At a village wedding in Galilee, Jesus, his mother Mary, and his new disciples are all guests. Partway through the feast the wine runs out, which in that honor-conscious culture would be an acute humiliation for the host family. Mary goes to her son. The six large stone jars standing nearby at the door were meant for ceremonial washings; Jesus has them filled with water, and sends a sample to the master of the feast. The sign — the first of seven 'signs' in John — opens Jesus's public ministry. Source: John 2 KJV.

the-sermon-on-the-mount-and-the-beatitud.context_blurb: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus climbs a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, and before he begins his longest single teaching he takes the posture a rabbi always used when teaching students. The sermon that follows runs three chapters and contains some of the most famous lines of Western literature — the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, the lily of the field, the Golden Rule, and the house built on sand. Source: Matthew 5–7 KJV.

the-sower-and-the-mustard-seed.context_blurb: Jesus pushes a small fishing boat a little way out from the shore of the Sea of Galilee, sits down in it while the crowd stands on the beach, and opens a parable with a farmer image. Later in the same chapter he gives another parable about the smallest of all garden seeds growing into a tree where the birds come and lodge. The 'kingdom of heaven' chain in Matthew 13 and Mark 4 is one of Jesus's great teaching sequences. Source: Matthew 13; Mark 4 KJV.

the-good-samaritan-on-the-jericho-road.context_blurb: A lawyer tries to test Jesus by asking who exactly counts as his 'neighbor.' Jesus answers with a story. He sets it on a specific road — a man traveling downhill from Jerusalem — a road that dropped more than three thousand feet in just over fifteen miles, perfect ambush country. Three different people pass the half-dead victim before the one who finally stops. Source: Luke 10:25–37 KJV.

the-prodigal-son-the-ring-the-sandals-an.context_blurb: In Luke 15 Jesus tells a parable that opens with a plain one-line setup: 'A certain man had two sons.' The younger boy walks up to his father one morning with a demand that would have shocked every listener at the time. He goes off to a far country, spends what his father gave him, ends up feeding animals Jews considered unclean — and finally comes to himself, rehearsing a short speech on the long walk home. The father's answer and the complaint of the older brother who stayed are the heart of the parable. Source: Luke 15:11–32 KJV.

the-lost-sheep-and-the-lost-coin.context_blurb: In Luke 15 Jesus tells three parables that are all about finding what was lost. The first is a shepherd who has a hundred sheep and finds that one has strayed. The second is a woman with ten silver coins who sweeps the whole house for the one that fell out of her head-dress. Each parable ends the same way — joy, calling in the neighbors, the simple triumphant line that heaven rejoices in the same way. Source: Luke 15:1–10 KJV.

lazarus-and-dives-and-the-sheep-and-the-.context_blurb: Jesus tells a parable in Luke 16 about two men who die on the same day. One is a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen who feasts every day at his own table; the other is a poor beggar covered in sores who lies outside the rich man's gate hoping for the scraps that fall. The parable turns everything upside down after death. In Matthew 25 Jesus gives another vision of the final judgment — a shepherd separating two kinds of animal — that has worked on Christian imagination ever since. Sources: Luke 16; Matthew 25 KJV.

the-talents-and-the-ten-virgins.context_blurb: In a pair of parables in Matthew 25, Jesus tells of a rich man who entrusts different sums of money to three of his servants before a long journey, and of ten young women waiting at night with lamps for a bridegroom's wedding procession. Both are parables about being ready. Source: Matthew 25:1–30 KJV.

come-forth-raising-jairuss-daughter-and-.context_blurb:
The gospels tell several stories of Jesus raising the dead, and two of the best known come from Mark and from John. In Mark a twelve-year-old girl dies while her father is still pleading for help; in John a grown man has already lain for days in his tomb when Jesus arrives.

In Mark's gospel a synagogue ruler named Jairus pushed through the crowd, threw himself down before Jesus and begged him to come and lay hands on his little daughter, who was dying at home.

Before they reached the house the girl had died, and hired mourners were wailing. When Jesus told them she was not dead but sleeping, they laughed him to scorn, so he put them all outside and went in with only the parents and three of his disciples.

He took the dead girl by the hand and spoke to her in Aramaic, the everyday language of Galilee: Talitha cumi. Mark, writing in Greek, explains that the words mean little girl, get up. She rose and walked about the room while her parents stared. Jesus's last instruction was strikingly ordinary: he told them that she should be given something to eat.

John's gospel tells a slower and larger story. In Bethany, a village two miles from Jerusalem, lived Lazarus and his two sisters, Martha and Mary, and when Lazarus fell ill the sisters sent word to Jesus, their friend. This Mary is Mary of Bethany, not Mary Magdalene and not the mother of Jesus. Jesus deliberately waited, and by the time he came Lazarus had lain in the tomb four days; when Jesus ordered the stone taken away, Martha warned him that by now the body would stink. Then Jesus called into the tomb for Lazarus to come forth, and the dead man walked out in his grave clothes.

teaches.3b77deba50: When Jesus told them she was not dead but sleeping, they laughed him to scorn, so he put them all outside and went in with only the parents and three of his disciples.

five-loaves-and-two-fishes-feeding-the-f.context_blurb: Late one afternoon on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, a huge crowd has followed Jesus into a lonely, grassy place and has nothing to eat. The disciples want to send them home to buy supper; Jesus tells them to feed the crowd themselves. The miracle begins with the lunch of one small boy and ends with a specific count of baskets gathered afterwards. The scene is the only one of Jesus's miracles that all four gospels record. Sources: Matthew 14; Mark 6; Luke 9; John 6 KJV.

the-storm-on-the-sea-and-walking-on-the-.context_blurb: The disciples Peter, Andrew, James, and John worked as commercial fishermen on the same lake Jesus later crossed many times with them. On one crossing Jesus slept through a violent storm in the stern of their boat; the terrified disciples woke him. On another night the disciples were in the boat alone when a figure walked out across the waves toward them, and Peter asked to walk out and meet him. Sources: Mark 4:35–41; Matthew 14:22–33 KJV.

the-paralytic-through-the-roof-and-blind.context_blurb: Jesus is teaching inside a packed house in Capernaum, and four men arrive carrying a paralysed friend on his sleeping mat. The crowd at the door is too tight to push through — so they find another way in. Later in Mark's gospel, Jesus is leaving the city of Jericho surrounded by a huge following when a blind beggar sitting by the road hears who is passing and shouts out his own name over and over, refusing to be hushed. Sources: Mark 2; Mark 10 KJV.

the-transfiguration-on-the-mountain.context_blurb: The gospels say Jesus led a small group of his closest disciples up a high mountain, apart from the rest. There his clothes began to shine, and two long-dead figures from the Hebrew Bible appeared with him on the mountainside. A cloud came and covered them, and a voice spoke out of the cloud. The three disciples came down the mountain in silence. Sources: Matthew 17; Mark 9; Luke 9 KJV.

palm-sunday-and-the-whip-of-cords.context_blurb: On the Sunday before his death, Jesus sends two disciples ahead of him into a village just outside Jerusalem to find and bring back a particular animal tied up near a door. He rides down the Mount of Olives into the city on it as the crowds spread cloaks and branches on the road. Days later, in the Temple itself, he drives out the money-changers and the sellers of sacrificial animals with a scourge of small cords. Sources: Matthew 21; John 2 KJV.

the-last-supper-the-kiss-and-let-this-cu.context_blurb: In an upper room in Jerusalem on the night before Passover, Jesus eats the Passover meal with the Twelve. Partway through the meal he tells them that one of the men eating with him will betray him, and as they go around the table they each begin to ask the same short, worried question. Later that same night in a garden across the Kidron Valley, Jesus prays three times under the olive trees while his closest three disciples cannot stay awake, and the betrayer finally arrives at the head of an arresting party with a single pre-arranged signal. Sources: Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18 KJV.

peters-denial-and-the-cock-crowing.context_blurb: On the night Jesus is arrested and taken to the high priest's house for questioning, one of his closest disciples follows the arresting party at a distance and slips into the courtyard. The servants and guards there have kindled a fire against the cold, and the disciple stands among them warming his hands. Three different people recognise him through the course of the night, and each time he insists he does not know Jesus — until a bird crows just before dawn. The last scene of John's gospel reconciles the same disciple to Jesus by a very similar charcoal fire. Sources: Matthew 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18, 21 KJV.

pilate-the-crown-of-thorns-and-what-is-t.context_blurb: Dragged by the Jewish authorities at dawn to the Roman governor's residence in Jerusalem, Jesus is questioned by the Roman prefect of Judea. The governor's opening question cuts straight to the political charge: 'Art thou the King of the Jews?' Jesus does not deny it. The soldiers plait a crown out of thorn-branches, dress him in a scarlet robe, and the governor finally offers the crowd a choice between Jesus and a prisoner named Barabbas. Sources: Matthew 27; John 18–19 KJV.

simon-of-cyrene-the-seven-last-words-and.context_blurb: On the walk out of Jerusalem toward the execution ground, Jesus is too exhausted to carry the crossbeam alone. Roman soldiers grab a random bystander from the crowd and force him to shoulder it. Mark's gospel names him in one phrase. At the hill called Golgotha a sign in three languages is hung above the cross, and across the three hours of darkness the four gospels together record a handful of famous last sayings — including a Hebrew cry from Psalm 22 and a single Greek word meaning 'it is finished.' Sources: Mark 15; John 19 KJV.

joseph-of-arimathea-and-the-empty-tomb.context_blurb: The afternoon of the crucifixion, a wealthy member of the Jewish ruling council walks in to see the Roman governor Pilate and boldly asks for the body of Jesus. Mark's gospel calls him 'an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God.' He takes the body down, wraps it in a linen sheet, and lays it in his own new-cut rock tomb in a garden nearby. Early on the first morning after the Sabbath, three women walk to that tomb carrying spices — and find the great stone already rolled away. Sources: Mark 15–16; John 19–20 KJV.

emmaus-doubting-thomas-and-the-153-fish.context_blurb: After the resurrection, two of Jesus's followers are walking home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus about seven miles away. A stranger falls in beside them and walks and talks with them for nearly the whole seven miles — and they never realise who he is until he breaks bread at their table that evening. Days later, in another appearance, Jesus comes through locked doors to the Eleven and the once-doubting disciple Thomas sees him for himself. The last chapter of John takes the risen Jesus back to the shore of the Sea of Tiberias and a charcoal fire. Sources: Luke 24; John 20–21 KJV.

andrew-and-the-x-shaped-cross-of-patras.context_blurb:
Andrew, brother of Simon Peter, was a fisherman from Galilee. The Gospel of John makes him one of the earliest men to follow Jesus, and later Christian tradition follows him to a cross in Greece and his bones to a cold northern shore, where the shape of his cross still flies on a nation's flag.

Andrew began as a disciple of John the Baptist. One day beside the Jordan he and another of John's followers went after Jesus and stayed with him until evening, and the first thing Andrew did afterwards was hurry off to find his brother Simon, the man Jesus would rename Peter, and bring him to Jesus.

What Andrew told Simon is one of the first announcements in the gospel story: he and his friend had found the Messias, the Greek form of the word Messiah. In John's gospel it is Andrew, not Peter, who speaks that word first. Because he answered before any of the others, the Greek Orthodox churches give Andrew a title no other apostle shares: Protokletos, the First-Called.

John's gospel gives Andrew one more quiet, practical moment. A crowd of some five thousand had trailed Jesus out to a deserted spot by the Sea of Galilee and found itself without food. It was Andrew who noticed a boy carrying five barley loaves and two small fish and brought him forward, wondering aloud what so little could do among so many, and from that small offering came the feeding of the whole crowd.

Later tradition sends Andrew preaching through Greece until he was condemned to crucifixion at Patras. He was not nailed to an upright cross like the one Jesus died on but bound to one shaped like an X, the shape heralds call a saltire, and ever since it has carried his name as Saint Andrew's Cross. The story that Andrew asked not to die on the same shape as his master is a later Western legend, but the X is the shape that stuck.

A medieval legend says a monk named Regulus carried some of Andrew's bones by sea, was shipwrecked on the coast of Fife, and founded the town later called Saint Andrews. Scotland chose Andrew as its patron, put his white cross on a blue ground as its flag, and marks Saint Andrew's Day, the thirtieth of November, as its national holiday.

bartholomew-flayed-alive-in-armenia.context_blurb:
Bartholomew was one of the twelve apostles Jesus chose, a man the gospels barely describe. Later Christian legend made up for that silence: it sent him east to preach, gave him one of the most horrifying martyrdoms in the saints' stories, and turned his flayed skin into one of the strangest images in Western art.

Matthew, Mark and Luke each give a list of the twelve, and in all three Bartholomew's name follows Philip's, as though the two were partners. His feast falls on 24 August, one of the oldest apostle days in the Christian calendar.

The name Bartholomew is really a family label, not a given name. In Aramaic, the language Jesus and his followers spoke, it means son of Tolmai. John's gospel never mentions a Bartholomew, but it pairs Philip with a disciple called Nathanael, and since the two names never appear in the same gospel, Christian scholars often take Nathanael and Bartholomew to be one man.

An early tradition sent Bartholomew east as far as India. The later and stronger tradition, standard from the medieval Golden Legend onward, sent him to Greater Armenia, high in the mountains beyond Persia, where he won over its king, Polymius, and baptised him at Albanopolis. No Armenian king list knows a Polymius, so the tale is legend, but Armenia became the traditional place of his death. It was not the king who killed him. The king's brother, Prince Astyages, furious at the conversion, had the apostle seized and put to death.

The Golden Legend and centuries of painters tell how: Astyages had him skinned alive and then beheaded, and in old paintings Bartholomew carries the knife that did it. Other traditions say he was crucified or simply beheaded, but the flaying is the version the West remembered. Because of that death, butchers, tanners and leather-workers, whose trades all deal in skin and hide, took Bartholomew as their patron saint.

Michelangelo gave the legend its strangest image. In the 1530s he painted the Last Judgment across the altar wall of Rome's Sistine Chapel, with Bartholomew among the saints around Christ, holding up his own empty skin. The face on that sagging skin is Michelangelo's own: the artist painted himself as a hollow pelt in a flayed saint's hand. Scholars read it as anything from a prayer for mercy to a bitter protest at being made to paint the wall.

matthew-the-tax-collector-at-the-receipt.context_blurb: One of Jesus's twelve apostles had a job before he was called that made his neighbours despise him: he sat at a customs booth on the trade road by the Sea of Galilee, collecting taxes for Rome. Jesus walked past, said two words, and the man got up and left his table. The scene has been painted many times — most famously by Caravaggio, in a huge canvas for a chapel in the French church in Rome. By tradition the same man wrote the first of the four gospels in the New Testament. Sources: Matthew 9:9; Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27 KJV.

philip-and-nathanael-under-the-fig-tree.context_blurb: The day after John the Baptist first pointed Jesus out at the Jordan, Jesus met a young man from Bethsaida — the same fishing town as Peter and Andrew — and called him with two words: 'Follow me.' This young apostle immediately went to find his skeptical friend sitting under a tree and brought him to Jesus. Jesus greeted the friend as an Israelite in whom there was no guile, and said he had seen him under that tree before the two of them ever met. Source: John 1:43–51 KJV.

thomas-the-twin-put-your-finger-here-and.context_blurb: One of Jesus's twelve apostles is introduced in the Gospel of John by a Greek nickname that means 'the twin.' He is the disciple who was not with the others on the first Easter evening when the risen Jesus appeared in the locked room, and who refuses to believe them. A week later Jesus comes back through the door with him there, and offers him the physical sign he had demanded. Later Christian tradition carries this apostle farther east than any of the others, as far as the Malabar Coast of India. Sources: John 20:24–29 KJV; Acts of Thomas.

simon-the-zealot-and-thaddaeus-the-two-l.context_blurb: Every Gospel list of the Twelve Apostles ends the same way: two names paired together just before Judas Iscariot. The second-to-last is a Simon — not Peter, a different one — carrying a one-word tag that would eventually become his standard name. The one just ahead of him is a figure called Thaddaeus (and in some lists Lebbaeus or Judas not Iscariot). Later tradition pairs them together on missionary journeys; one of them becomes the great Western patron of lost or impossible causes. Sources: Matthew 10; Mark 3; Luke 6 KJV.

james-son-of-zebedee-the-first-apostle-k.context_blurb: The apostle James, son of Zebedee, worked with his father and his brother John in a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee before Jesus called them. Jesus gave the two brothers together a joint Aramaic nickname — 'sons of thunder.' In the book of Acts, King Herod Agrippa I begins persecuting the Jerusalem church and has this apostle killed by the sword. He becomes the very first of the Twelve to die for his faith. Later Spanish legend brings his body to the far northwest corner of Iberia, where a famous pilgrimage shrine still bears his name. Sources: Mark 1:19; Acts 12 KJV.

james-the-just-the-fullers-club-at-the-t.context_blurb: A man named James, called 'the Just' or 'the Righteous,' is identified in Mark 6:3 as a brother of Jesus of Nazareth. In the book of Acts he becomes the chief figure of the Jerusalem church — the one Peter and Paul report to, and the one who finally decides the Gentile question at the Jerusalem Council. By tradition he wore no wool, drank no wine, and had calloused knees from a lifetime of kneeling to pray. Josephus and the second-century historian Hegesippus both record his violent death. Sources: Acts 15; Josephus Antiquities 20.

judas-iscariot-the-thirty-pieces-the-kis.context_blurb: One of Jesus's twelve disciples went in the week of Passover to the chief priests and arranged to hand Jesus over to them, for a price that Matthew's gospel takes straight from the prophet Zechariah. In the garden of Gethsemane the betrayal is sealed with a pre-arranged signal — a single gesture at close range. Matthew and Acts give two different versions of what happens to the money and to the betrayer afterwards; both end in a field known locally by an Aramaic name meaning 'the field of blood.' Sources: Matthew 26–27; Acts 1; Zechariah 11 KJV.

peters-chains-the-angel-in-the-cell-and-.context_blurb: In the book of Acts, King Herod Agrippa I has just put the apostle James the son of Zebedee to death with a sword, and seeing that this pleased the people he also arrests Peter and locks him up in prison chained between two soldiers, with four squads of soldiers assigned to guard him in turn. During the night an angel appears in the cell, taps Peter awake, and leads him out. Meanwhile the Jerusalem church is praying for him at the house of Mary the mother of John Mark — and a young servant-girl named Rhoda is the first to hear his knock at the gate. Source: Acts 12 KJV.

pentecost-the-wind-the-fire-and-the-thre.context_blurb: Fifty days after Passover, in the opening chapters of the book of Acts, about a hundred and twenty followers of Jesus are shut in a single upper room in Jerusalem. A sudden sound as of a rushing mighty wind fills the house, and a flame as of a small tongue of fire comes to rest over the head of each of them. They go out into the street and begin to speak, and every one of the pilgrim visitors in Jerusalem for the feast hears his own home-language. One of the Twelve stands up with the Eleven to preach to the whole crowd. Source: Acts 1–2 KJV.

stephen-the-first-martyr-and-the-young-m.context_blurb: In the early Jerusalem church, the apostles are overwhelmed and pick seven men to handle the daily food-distribution to the widows so that they themselves can keep preaching. Acts 6 names the very first of these seven — a man 'full of faith and of the Holy Ghost' — and the long speech he gives before the Sanhedrin in Acts 7 is the longest in the book. His execution follows at once, and a young Pharisee named Saul of Tarsus is standing nearby holding the coats of the men who throw the stones. Source: Acts 6–7 KJV.

peter-and-john-at-the-beautiful-gate-sil.context_blurb: In the book of Acts chapter 3, two of Jesus's apostles walk up together to the Temple in Jerusalem for the afternoon prayer, as they did every day. A man who has been lame since birth is laid daily at the gate called Beautiful to ask alms of the people going in. The two apostles stop, Peter speaks a famous line about silver and gold, and the man rises and goes into the Temple leaping and praising God. The Sanhedrin then arrests them for the night. Source: Acts 3 KJV.

the-damascus-road-the-light-the-voice-an.context_blurb: Before he was the apostle Paul, Saul of Tarsus was on the road hunting Christians. He carried official letters from the high priest in Jerusalem authorising him to arrest any followers of Jesus he could find in the synagogues of a particular city and drag them back in chains. On the way a sudden light from heaven knocked him to the ground and a voice spoke. The scene is told three times in Acts and remembered forever as the pattern of a sudden conversion. Sources: Acts 9, 22, 26 KJV.

the-jerusalem-council-and-the-split-of-p.context_blurb: At Antioch some men who had come down from Judea began teaching the Gentile converts that they could not be saved unless they also kept the full Law of Moses. The dispute was so sharp that Paul and Barnabas were sent down to Jerusalem to settle it with the apostles and elders. Acts 15 tells of the great council that followed and the letter the Jerusalem leaders sent back out to the Gentile churches. The same chapter ends with a sharp quarrel between Paul and Barnabas over whether to take John Mark along on a second journey. Source: Acts 15 KJV.

paul-at-the-areopagus-the-altar-to-the-u.context_blurb: Paul reaches Athens alone, waiting for Silas and Timothy to catch up. He walks the streets of the city, and one sight above all others stirs him up — the countless altars and statues on every corner. He is invited to speak at the Areopagus, the open-air court on a rocky hill below the Acropolis, where Epicurean and Stoic philosophers are curious about his teaching. He opens from an altar he had seen in the city and quotes a line from the Cretan poet Epimenides. Source: Acts 17:16–34 KJV.

paul-and-silas-midnight-singing-the-phil.context_blurb: In the Macedonian city of Philippi, a slave girl follows the apostle Paul and his companion Silas through the streets for days, shouting after them. She is possessed by a particular kind of spirit, and when Paul finally commands it out of her, her owners drag the two missionaries into the market-square. By nightfall Paul and Silas are stripped, beaten with rods, locked in the inner prison with their feet in the stocks — and singing hymns at midnight. An earthquake opens every door. Source: Acts 16 KJV.

paul-before-agrippa-and-festus-almost-th.context_blurb: After his arrest in the Temple at Jerusalem, Paul is held for two years in Roman custody at the Mediterranean port that served as the governor's headquarters in Judea. His case passes from one Roman governor to another and finally comes before the local Jewish king Herod Agrippa II and his sister Berenice. Paul tells his conversion-story for the third time in Acts, and Agrippa gives the famous half-answer that has become a proverb. Source: Acts 24–26 KJV.

shipwreck-on-malta-the-alexandrian-grain.context_blurb: In the autumn of about 60 CE Paul, still a prisoner, is being shipped from Caesarea to Rome under a Roman centurion named Julius. While the ship is at Fair Havens on the south coast of Crete, Paul warns against sailing on so late in the season. The centurion overrules him, a storm catches the ship, and the fourteen-day drift ends in shipwreck on a small Mediterranean island. The whole party reaches shore alive. The island's chief Publius takes them in. Source: Acts 27–28 KJV.

paul-beheaded-on-the-ostian-way.context_blurb: The book of Acts ends with Paul in Rome under a light form of house arrest, in his own rented house, receiving all who came and preaching freely. Acts does not describe his death. Later Christian tradition — Tertullian, Eusebius, and the Liber Pontificalis — places it under the emperor Nero and executes him by the sword rather than by the cross because of his Roman citizenship. His tomb is now covered by the great Roman basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls on the Ostian Way, and his feast is kept the same day as Peter's. Source: Acts 28; Tertullian, De Praescriptione.

john-on-patmos-the-four-horsemen-and-the.context_blurb: At the end of the first century, by Christian tradition, the aged apostle John was exiled by the Roman emperor Domitian to a small rocky island in the eastern Aegean for refusing to burn incense to the emperor. There he wrote down a long series of visions that became the last book of the Bible. The seven churches of Asia Minor, the four riders on four coloured horses, the woman clothed with the sun fleeing a great red dragon, and the new Jerusalem coming down out of heaven are all in that book. Source: Revelation 1–21 KJV.

peter-crucified-upside-down-at-rome.context_blurb: By the end of his life, Christian tradition places the fisherman apostle Peter far from Galilee, leading the small Christian community in Rome itself. His first epistle sends greetings from 'Babylon,' which early Christians read as a code-name for Rome. In the summer of 64 CE the emperor Nero burned Christians to clear his own blame for the great fire of Rome; by tradition Peter was martyred in that persecution on the Vatican hill in a particular posture he had asked for because he counted himself unworthy to die the same way as Jesus. In 1968 Pope Paul VI announced that the bones under the high altar of St Peter's were almost certainly his. Source: 1 Peter 5; Eusebius 2.

the-silversmiths-of-ephesus-and-the-riot.context_blurb: In the city of Ephesus the apostle Paul rents out a lecture hall and teaches in it daily for two full years. The whole province hears him. The silversmiths of Ephesus, who make a living casting silver souvenirs of the great temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — see their business falling off and start a riot. For two hours the mob in the theater of Ephesus shouts the same line in Greek over and over, until the town clerk finally calms them. Source: Acts 19 KJV.

aphrodite-born-from-the-sea-foam.context_blurb:
Love and beauty belong to Aphrodite among the Greek gods, and her birth is the strangest of any Olympian. The poet Hesiod, in his Theogony, has her rise full-grown out of the sea, while Homer gives her an ordinary divine family. Rome took over her stories, and a Renaissance painter made her arrival from the waves one of the most famous pictures in the world.

The Romans, who retold the Greek myths under Latin names, called her Venus, and the planet Venus still carries that name. Her bird is the dove: doves perch on her statues, draw her chariot in later art and nestle in pairs at her feet.

Hesiod's story begins in violence. The Titan Cronus attacked his father, the sky god Ouranos, with a sickle and flung what he cut away far out to sea. White foam spread where it fell, and from the foam rose Aphrodite, already grown; Hesiod even draws her name from aphros, the Greek word for foam. The west wind, Zephyr, carried her across the water to the little island of Cythera and then on to Cyprus, and from that landing she took her titles Cypris, the Lady of Cyprus, and Cytherea. Her temple at Paphos on Cyprus became one of the great shrines of the ancient world.

Artists from ancient times onward pictured her coming ashore standing on a scallop shell, and the shell became her emblem. Centuries later the same scallop became the badge of Christian pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela, a curious echo between traditions. Where she stepped onto the beach, Hesiod says, fresh grass sprang up from the soil under her bare feet, and painters ever since have added roses and myrtle around her.

The goddess of love made a stormy wife. In Homer's Odyssey, a bard sings how her husband Hephaestus, the lame smith of the gods, caught her with her lover Ares, the god of war, under a net of golden threads finer than a spider's web, then called all the gods in to laugh at the pair. She also owned a girdle, an embroidered sash whose magic left anyone who looked at the wearer helpless with love. In Book 14 of the Iliad, Hera borrowed it to beguile Zeus on Mount Ida, so that he would look away from the war while the Greeks won back ground.

Not every poet agreed on how she was born. In Homer's Iliad, when the mortal hero Diomedes wounds Aphrodite in battle, she flees to Olympus weeping and is comforted by her mother, Dione, for Homer makes her simply the daughter of Zeus and Dione. Plato later treated the two, the heavenly foam-born goddess and Homer's daughter of Zeus, as two different Aphrodites.

Around 1485 the Florentine painter Sandro Botticelli painted her arrival from the sea. His Birth of Venus, which hangs in Florence's Uffizi, still shapes how the West imagines her.

apollo-at-delphi-the-python-and-the-pyth.context_blurb:
Apollo is the shining Greek god of music, prophecy and the bow. His shrine at Delphi, high on the mountainside of Parnassus, was the greatest oracle of the ancient world, where kings and cities came for answers. The Homeric Hymn to Apollo and later poets tell how he was born, how he won Delphi, and what that victory cost him.

Apollo and his twin sister Artemis, the huntress of the forests, were children of Zeus and the Titaness Leto. Hera, jealous, ordered every land to refuse Leto a place to give birth, and Leto wandered without shelter. In the end Delos, a little floating island that Hera's ban on land could not bind, took her in and fastened itself to the seabed, and there, clutching a palm tree, Leto bore her twins.

Hera had also set a monstrous she-serpent, Python, to plague Leto, and the young Apollo went after it in its cleft in the rocks of Parnassus and brought it down with his arrows. The Homeric Hymn says the name comes from a Greek word meaning to rot, because the serpent's body rotted where it fell. Apollo claimed the place as his own, and it became Delphi, the oracle the whole Greek world consulted, where envoys of kings and cities came asking whether to go to war, whom to marry and where to plant a colony. The Greeks called it the navel of the world.

At Delphi the god spoke through a priestess, the Pythia. She sat on a tripod, a three-legged bronze seat placed over a crack in the rock where holy vapours were believed to rise, and copies of the tripod were the proudest prizes at every great Greek sanctuary. Before she prophesied, the Pythia chewed the leaves of Apollo's sacred plant, the laurel. The nymph Daphne, fleeing from Apollo, had been turned into the first laurel tree, so the god wore her leaves ever after, broke his first branches in the Vale of Tempe, where he went to be purified after killing the serpent, and crowned his victors with laurel wreaths.

Over the temple door every pilgrim read two short commands: know yourself, and nothing to excess. Greek tradition credited both sayings to the Seven Sages, and the first became the motto of Greek philosophy.

The god's answers could cut both ways. Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia, sent gold to Delphi and asked how a war against Persia would go. The priestess replied that a great empire would fall if he marched across the river Halys. He crossed, Cyrus of Persia crushed his army and took his capital, and the great empire Croesus destroyed turned out to be Lydia, his own.

Even a god could be made to serve. Zeus once sentenced Apollo to a term as a hired hand in the house of King Admetus of Pherae, and the god of music spent it minding the king's cattle out in the fields. Some tellings blame the blood shed at Delphi; Apollodorus says it was punishment for killing the Cyclopes. Apollo grew so fond of his master that he later persuaded the Fates to spare Admetus on the day he was meant to die.

arachne-the-weaver-challenging-athena.context_blurb:
In Book 6 of Ovid's Metamorphoses, a young Lydian weaver named Arachne grows so proud of her skill that she boasts it matches Athena's, and she refuses to admit she owes anything to the goddess who invented weaving. Athena comes to her disguised as an old woman to warn her, then throws off the disguise, and the two sit down at their looms side by side.

Athena wove the gods in glory. At the centre of her tapestry she showed her own contest with Poseidon for the city of Athens: he struck the rock of the Acropolis with his trident and a salt spring gushed out, she struck it and an olive tree grew, and the people chose her gift. In the corners she wove warnings, mortals turned into mountains and birds for challenging the gods.

Arachne wove the gods in shame: twenty-one scenes of gods taking the shapes of animals and other things to trick and carry off mortal women. Zeus appears in more of them than any other god, in nine scenes, as a swan, an eagle, a shower of gold and more. The most famous panel showed Zeus as a great white bull on the shore of Sidon, kneeling so that the princess Europa could climb onto his back, then plunging into the sea and swimming her away to Crete. The continent of Europe carries her name.

Arachne's work was flawless. Athena, goddess of every craft, could not find a single fault in it, and that was more than she could bear: she tore the tapestry, with its pictures of the gods' crimes, to shreds with her bare hands. Then she snatched up the shuttle, the boxwood tool that carries the thread back and forth across the loom, and struck Arachne on the forehead with it, three times and then a fourth. The humiliation was too much for Arachne. She knotted a noose from her own thread and hanged herself.

Athena wet her with drops from a herb of Hecate and bade her live and go on hanging. The girl shrivelled: hair, nose and ears dropped away, her head dwindled almost to nothing, and her fingers turned into thin legs clinging to her sides. Arachne had become a spider, spinning her thread to this day. Her name is simply the ancient Greek word for spider, and the scientific class Arachnida takes its name from her story.

ares-reviled-the-war-god-the-gods-hate.context_blurb:
Ares is the Greek god of war, but not of war's planning, which belongs to wise Athena. He is the god of the battlefield's raw fury and slaughter, and Homer's Iliad hardly hides its contempt for him: Zeus himself tells him he is the most hateful of all the gods on Olympus.

Where Athena guards the craft and strategy of war, Ares, son of Zeus and Hera, loves the rage and the bloodshed for their own sake. He seldom rides into battle alone. Beside him go his two sons by Aphrodite, Deimos and Phobos, whose names mean Terror and Fear, and with them runs Enyo, the sacker of cities.

In Book 5 of the Iliad a mortal humbles him. The Greek hero Diomedes, with Athena herself driving his spear, stabs Ares in the belly, and the war god flees to Olympus to whimper to his father. Zeus gives him no comfort, only the verdict that he is the most hateful of the gods.
