teaches.273c50c4bd: He was only a boy, with no stomach for killing the mightiest warrior alive, so his brothers cooked him a stew of wolf and serpent flesh with beer to make him savage.
teaches.370c8a66bb: Sigurd woke to the death-blow, snatched up his own sword, Gram, the blade that had killed Fafnir, and hurled it after the fleeing killer.
teaches.10841ad18a: As she died she asked to be burned on Sigurd's own pyre, with Gram laid bare between their bodies as it had lain between them on the night he came to her in Gunnar's shape.
teaches.bec06b3864: Gotterdammerung, the Twilight of the Gods, the fourth and last of its operas, first staged in 1876, closes with the hero's murder and the queen's fire.
teaches.135b7c9597: Gram caught Guttorm between the shoulders and cut him clean in two, so that one half fell forward out of the room and the other fell back inside it.

draupnir-odins-ring-that-drips-eight-mor.context_blurb:
Odin, chief of the Norse gods, wore a gold arm-ring of dwarf-work, one of the great named treasures of Norse myth. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda tells where it came from and what it did, and the ring turns up again at a funeral and a courtship.

Its name was Draupnir, the dripper, because new gold rings kept falling from it like drops of water from a wet blade. Snorri gives the exact schedule: every ninth night, eight new rings of equal weight dropped from it. Nine runs all through Norse myth, from the nine worlds to Odin's nine nights on the world-tree.

The dwarf brothers Sindri and Brokkr made it after Loki bet his own head on a contest of smithcraft. Loki lost and wriggled out on a technicality, saying the dwarves could take his head but not his neck, so Brokkr stitched Loki's lips together instead.

When Baldr, Odin's beloved son, lay dead on his funeral ship, Odin laid Draupnir on the pyre beside him, his last gift to his son.

The ring appears again in the Eddic poem Skirnismal. The god Freyr fell in love with Gerd, a giantess of Jotunheim, and dispatched Skirnir, his servant, to win her with eleven golden apples and Draupnir itself; she scorned the gold and yielded only to the threat of a curse.

fimbulwinter-three-winters-with-no-summe.context_blurb: In Norse mythology, the world does not end quietly. Almost every named Aesir god dies in one great final battle, the sky splits, and the sea rises to swallow the earth. The Voluspa poem of the Poetic Edda and Snorri's Prose Edda both describe the long run-up — a great winter with no summer between, a wolf-age of men who kill their own kin, and a specific wolf that at last catches and swallows the sun it has been chasing across the sky. Sources: Voluspa; Snorri's Gylfaginning.

freyja-cats-falcon-cloak-and-the-brising.context_blurb: In Norse myth the goddess Freyja of the Vanir came to live in Asgard after the war between the Aesir and the Vanir. She is the great goddess of love and gold, half-sister of Freyr, and her chariot is pulled by two great animals of a kind no other god drives. She owns a falcon-cloak that any god may borrow to fly in. The story of how she bought her signature necklace from four dwarves is one of the strangest in the Prose Edda. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda; Lokasenna.

freyr-the-sword-he-traded-for-love.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the god of sunshine, good weather, harvest, and peace is not one of the Aesir by birth. He belongs to the older tribe of gods — the Vanir — who were traded to the Aesir as hostages after their war. His greatest treasure is a magic sword that fights by itself. But in the poem Skirnismal he climbs onto Odin's seat Hlidskjalf and sees a giantess he cannot stop thinking about, and sends his servant Skirnir to woo her for him. The price he pays for her comes due at Ragnarok. Source: Skirnismal; Snorri's Prose Edda.

gleipnir-and-tyrs-hand-the-six-impossibl.context_blurb: In the Norse stories Loki has three monstrous children by the giantess Angrboda — the death-goddess Hel, a great serpent that will grow long enough to circle the whole world, and a third child that terrifies the Aesir most of all. The gods try to bind him twice with iron fetters named Leyding and Dromi, and both snap. The dwarves of Svartalfheim make them a third binding out of six things that do not exist — a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the breath of fish, and three more — and one god is willing to prove his good faith to the wolf by laying his hand in its jaws. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

gram-in-the-barnstokk-the-sword-only-sig.context_blurb: In the middle of King Volsung's great hall stands a living oak the family call Barnstokk — 'child-trunk' — with its branches spreading up through the roof-beams. On the night of Signy's wedding-feast a one-eyed stranger walks in and does one shocking thing to the tree before he leaves. Every warrior in the hall tries to pull his sword from the trunk, and only Sigmund — one of the youngest men there — can draw it out. The whole Volsung dynasty will carry the pieces of that sword forward. Source: Volsunga Saga ch. 3.

grendels-mother-in-the-mere-the-giant-sw.context_blurb: In the Old English poem Beowulf, the hero has torn off the arm of a monster named Grendel and hung it in the rafters of the mead-hall Heorot as a trophy. That same night a second monster comes to Heorot for revenge — Grendel's mother. Beowulf tracks her to her cave beneath a dark lake, and the fight at the bottom turns on a weapon not in his pack. Later tradition and the poem itself call his band of thanes 'the Geats.' Source: Beowulf.

grimhilds-potion-and-the-ride-through-th.context_blurb: The old king Gjuki of the Rhine has a queen who is far more dangerous than he is: a powerful sorceress who knows how to brew charmed drinks and speaks spells over them. She will engineer every disaster in the second half of the Volsunga Saga — a potion of forgetting handed to the hero, a swap of faces that lets another man cross the ring of fire in his shape, and the brothering oath that leads to Sigurd's murder in his own bed. Source: Volsunga Saga.

gullinbursti-the-golden-boar-that-lights.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the harvest-and-sunshine god of the Vanir owns a chariot pulled by a shining animal forged of solid gold. The dwarves Sindri and Brokkr made it in the great smithing-contest that produced the six treasures. Its name comes from its golden bristles, and it can swim through sea and run through air faster than any horse. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda; Skaldskaparmal.

gungnir-odins-spear-that-never-misses.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the All-Father Odin, chief of the Aesir and lord of the slain in Valhalla, carries a signature weapon into every battle — the same weapon he takes with him on his last ride out at Ragnarok. The dwarves called the Sons of Ivaldi forged it. It is also what Odin leaned on during his nine days hanging from the world-tree for the runes. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda; Havamal.

heimdallr-blows-the-gjallarhorn.context_blurb: In the Norse myths a shining god stands on the arch of the rainbow that joins the world of humans to the world of the gods. His whole duty is to watch: no giant may cross without his seeing it first. He drinks only pure mead, his hearing is so sharp he can hear grass growing on the earth, and when at last Ragnarok comes he lifts his great horn and blows a blast that every realm of the nine worlds hears. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

heimdallr-gjallarhorn-and-grass-growing.context_blurb: A rainbow bridge stretches from the world of humans up to the home of the gods. One god stands guard at its far end and lets no giant across. He sleeps less than a bird, sees a hundred leagues off as clearly by night as by day, and keeps his horn by him for the day of the last battle. In another old poem Rigsthula he walks among mortals under a different name and fathers the three classes of men. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Rigsthula.

heorot-the-hall-where-grendel-comes-at-n.context_blurb: The greatest surviving poem in the Old English language tells of a young warrior who sails across the sea to kill a hall-monster and, decades later, dies fighting a dragon. The whole first half is set in the mead-hall King Hrothgar built in Denmark, where the monster has haunted the night for twelve years. The poem itself survives in a single eleventh-century manuscript, Cotton Vitellius A.xv, from the British Library. Source: Beowulf.

hrungnir-the-whetstone-in-thors-forehead.context_blurb: In Snorri Sturluson's Skaldskaparmal, the strongest of all the giants has a stone heart, a stone head, a stone shield — his whole body is made of rock. He challenges Thor to single combat at a place called Griotunagard, and the giants build him a companion out of clay nine leagues tall to stand beside him. The duel ends with a whetstone lodged in Thor's forehead that a volva — the seeress Groa — later tries to chant out. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

huginn-and-muninn-thought-and-memory.context_blurb: Odin sits on his high seat in Asgard, but he cannot be in every corner of the world at once. To keep watch on all of Midgard he sends out two of the same kind of bird every dawn to fly the whole earth and come back at breakfast. Their names mean Thought and Memory. He also has two wolves named Geri and Freki beside his throne who eat his meat for him. He himself takes only wine. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Grimnismal.

idunns-apples-loki-the-eagle-and-the-kid.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the Aesir stay young because one goddess of Asgard keeps a wooden box of golden fruit and hands them around at every feast. The gods eat from her box; without it they would age like any mortal. In the story Snorri tells in Skaldskaparmal, Loki accidentally leads the giant Thjazi, in the shape of an eagle, straight into her garden — and then has to turn around and get her back. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

kvasir-and-the-mead-of-poetry-dwarves-bl.context_blurb: In the Norse origin of poetry itself, the two families of gods — the Aesir and the Vanir — ended their long war by sealing peace in one shared act at a great vat. Every god spat into it, and out of that spit grew a man named Kvasir, the wisest being alive. Two dwarves killed him and brewed his blood with honey into a magical mead that gave the gift of poetry to anyone who drank it. The giant Suttung took the mead for himself, and Odin went on a long trip to steal it back. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

lokasenna-the-flyting-at-aegirs-feast.context_blurb: In the Norse stories, one of the great banquet-hosts of the Aesir and Vanir is a sea-figure who brews ale in an enormous cauldron under the waves and invites the gods down to drink. The poem Lokasenna of the Poetic Edda sets Loki at that feast — hurling an insult at every god in turn and daring any of them to answer. Thor's final arrival ends the party. The sea-host's servants are also part of the story. Source: Lokasenna of the Poetic Edda.

lokis-brood-in-the-norse-imagination-kin.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the trickster Loki lives among the Aesir gods in Asgard, but Snorri opens his genealogy in the Prose Edda by pointing out that Loki is not one of the Aesir by blood at all. He is Odin's sworn brother, and that oath is what keeps him in Asgard. He has a loyal goddess wife named Sigyn and two sons by her; he also has three monstrous children by a giantess in Jotunheim; and once, as a mare, he mothered Odin's own eight-legged horse. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

lokis-lips-sewn-shut-the-head-forfeit-do.context_blurb: In Snorri's smithing-contest of the six treasures, two dwarf-brothers named Brokkr and Sindri compete against the dwarves called the Sons of Ivaldi for Loki's head. When the gods judge which of the six treasures is finest, the winning object goes to Thor — the war-hammer he will carry into every battle for the rest of Norse story. Loki tries to wriggle out of the wager on a technicality: Brokkr may not touch Loki's neck. Brokkr's answer, with his brother's awl, is one of the ugliest moments in the Prose Edda. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

lokis-punishment-bound-with-naris-entrai.context_blurb: Loki flees the wrath of the gods after the death of Baldr and hides in the mountains. He builds himself a paranoid house with one door on each of its four sides so that he can see every direction at once, and he turns into a salmon by day to swim in a waterfall. The gods catch him at last with a fishing-net he himself had just invented. His punishment is one of the darkest scenes in Norse myth — his loyal wife Sigyn sits with him in a cave with a wooden bowl, catching the venom that drips from a serpent fastened above him, until Ragnarok comes. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

mjolnir-the-hammer-of-thor.context_blurb: In Norse myth the red-bearded god of thunder rides across the sky in a chariot pulled by two goats, and the flash of his signature weapon is what people down in Midgard see as lightning. The dwarves Sindri and Brokkr forged it. It never misses what Thor throws it at, always returns to his hand, and the gods raise it to consecrate every funeral pyre. The small silver hammer-pendants hung around Viking necks have survived in great numbers. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda.

mjolnir-the-hammer-with-the-too-short-ha.context_blurb: In the Norse stories, Thor the thunder-god carries a single signature weapon that the Aesir gods count on above every other blade in Asgard when the giants of Jotunheim come down from the mountains. In the smithing-contest in which the dwarves Sindri and Brokkr forged it, Loki as a fly bit the dwarf's eye at a crucial moment — and the shortness of the hammer's handle was the result. Thor still kills the Midgard Serpent with it at Ragnarok. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal; Gylfaginning.

naglfar-the-ship-of-dead-mens-nails.context_blurb: In the Norse story of Ragnarok, the sea rises up over Midgard, the wolf Fenrir breaks loose, and a great ship sails out of the east across the flooded world, carrying an army of giants and monsters to the last battle. What that ship is made of is one of Snorri's grimmest details — and Snorri uses it to urge every Norseman to groom the dead before burial so as to delay the ship's finishing just a little longer. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

odin-against-fenrir-vidarrs-shoe-and-the.context_blurb: In the Norse story of the last battle, a monstrous wolf breaks loose after ages of being bound, and races across the world to devour the All-Father himself. Odin's silent son Vidarr is the one who finally answers him. Vidarr wears a huge boot of leather scraps trimmed from every boot ever made in Midgard — Snorri tells craftsmen to throw away such trimmings so Vidarr's shoe will be large enough. The scene at Ragnarok that follows is one of the most-painted in Norse mythology. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Vafthrudnismal.

odin-at-mimirs-well-trading-an-eye-for-a.context_blurb: The chief god of the Aesir in Norse myth is called the All-Father — lord of Asgard, master of poetry, war, and death. He is the father of Thor and the husband of Frigg. In Snorri's Prose Edda he once walks to the roots of the world-tree Yggdrasil, where a severed head keeps watch over a well of wisdom, and asks for a drink. The price the head demands is high. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

odin-on-yggdrasil-nine-nights-for-the-ru.context_blurb: Odin has already paid one eye at Mimir's well for a taste of wisdom, but he is still hungry for a deeper knowledge — the magical marks that shape fate itself, the ones gods and men still carve on stone and wood. In the poem Havamal of the Poetic Edda, he describes hanging on a windy tree, pierced by his own spear, given to himself, no bread, no drinking-horn, for nine nights. At the end of the ninth night he catches sight of what he came for and takes it screaming. Source: Havamal 138–145.

odin-the-wanderer-the-wild-hunt.context_blurb: In the Norse stories, one of the gods is often described walking the roads of Midgard disguised as an old man in a broad hat pulled down low, a grey-blue cloak, and a walking staff. He has only one eye, having traded the other long ago for a drink from Mimir's well. He rides an eight-legged horse that carries him between all the worlds. In Scandinavian folklore he still leads a shadowy band of hunters across the winter sky, a procession called the Oskoreia. Source: Snorri's Prose Edda; folklore.

regin-reforges-the-sword-gram-from-shard.context_blurb: In the Norse Volsunga Saga an old king dies in battle when his sword shatters against a stranger's spear — and he tells his young wife to keep the pieces for their unborn son. Years later that son grows up a foster-son of a cunning smith named Regin. Regin forges and reforges a sword from the shards, and the hero tests it by cleaving a block of iron down to its foundations. The whole arc behind the Volsung story also lies behind J. R. R. Tolkien's reforged sword in The Lord of the Rings. Source: Volsunga Saga.

sifs-golden-hair-the-prank-that-starts-t.context_blurb: In the Norse stories, Thor the thunder-god has a wife who lives with him in Asgard and is famous among the gods for one particular beauty. Poets say no woman in the nine worlds has ever had hair like hers — long and thick and golden, falling all the way to the ground. One day Loki, playing a cruel joke, cuts it all off in her sleep. The scene is the opening prank that triggers the whole smithing-contest among the dwarves — and the six great Norse treasures. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

sigurd-slays-fafnir-the-pit-and-the-upwa.context_blurb: In the Norse Volsunga Saga a young hero armed with his reforged father-sword Gram is sent by his foster-father Regin to kill a dragon coiled around a cursed hoard of gold on the moor called Gnitaheid. Regin tells him to dig a pit in the trail where the dragon slithers down to drink, and stab upward as the dragon passes over. Odin, meeting Sigurd in the shape of an old man, tells him to dig extra pits beside it to catch the poisonous blood. Source: Volsunga Saga; Fafnismal.

sigurd-tastes-the-dragons-blood-the-bird.context_blurb: In the Norse Volsunga Saga the young hero has just killed the dragon on Gnitaheid. His foster-father Regin sits down beside him, cuts one specific organ out of the dragon, and hands it to the boy with orders to cook it over the open fire while Regin lies down to sleep in the grass. When the hero burns a thumb on the roasting meat and sucks it, he suddenly understands the speech of birds — and the birds are talking about Regin. Source: Volsunga Saga; Fafnismal.

skidbladnir-the-ship-that-folds-into-a-p.context_blurb: Among the Norse gods, one of the Vanir who came to live in Asgard is the god of harvest, sunshine, and good weather — the god the farmers of Sweden and Norway prayed to for a peaceful year and a good crop. He owns a golden boar and a magic ship. The ship, forged by the dwarves called the Sons of Ivaldi, holds all the gods of Asgard together, always has a fair wind, and folds up small enough to carry in a pouch. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

sleipnir-loki-as-a-mare-and-odins-eight-.context_blurb: In Norse myth Odin the All-Father rides a great grey horse that can carry him between all the worlds, even down into the land of the dead. Snorri says this horse is stranger than any other horse ever born because of one feature of its body. The story of how it came to be — a bargain the Aesir made with a master builder for the walls of Asgard, and Loki's transformation into a mare — is told in Snorri's Gylfaginning. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Hyndluljod.

surtr-the-fire-giant-with-the-flaming-sw.context_blurb: In the Norse cosmos hung on the branches of the world-tree Yggdrasil, one of the nine worlds sits at the far southern edge, older than Asgard and older than the gods themselves — one of two primal worlds that existed before creation. A fire-giant stands at its border with a flaming sword, and at Ragnarok he leads the giants out against the gods and sets the whole universe on fire. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

the-master-builder-the-walls-of-asgard-f.context_blurb: In the Prose Edda a stranger arrives at the hall of the Norse gods and offers to build them a great stone rampart — one no giant will ever be able to break through. The gods ask his price, and the price turns out to be unthinkable. Loki promises he can get the wall built without the gods having to pay. The stranger has a stallion named Svadilfari who hauls stones for him, and Loki solves the problem with another transformation. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

the-norns-at-the-well-of-urd.context_blurb: In the Norse stories the whole cosmos hangs from one great tree with three roots — one reaching to the frost-giants, one to Hel, and one to the gods. Under a hall by a well at the gods' root live three fate-women who choose the life of every mortal and god. They carve runes on a stave of ash, water the roots of the tree with milk-coloured water, and keep the whole cosmos from rotting away. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

the-three-roosters-gullinkambi-fjalar-an.context_blurb: In the Voluspa of the Poetic Edda three roosters crow at the dawn of Ragnarok. One crows in Jotunheim to wake the giants, one crows in Asgard to wake the Aesir, and one crows down in Hel to wake the dead. The three birds between them wake up the whole universe for the last battle. Source: Voluspa.

the-wager-loki-bets-his-head-with-brokkr.context_blurb: In the Prose Edda Loki once cut off the golden hair of Thor's wife as a prank, and to save his own life he went down to the dwarf-quarter to have new hair made. His habit of bragging landed him in a much bigger scrape while he was there. He wagered against two more dwarves, Brokkr and Sindri, that they could not make three gifts to equal the three the first dwarves had already made for the gods. The three judges of the contest were the three heads of the Aesir pantheon. Source: Snorri's Skaldskaparmal.

thor-and-jormungandr-fishing-with-hymir.context_blurb: The Norse Midgard Serpent is the great sea-monster that wraps the whole world — so long he holds his own tail in his teeth. He is one of three monstrous children Loki fathered on the giantess Angrboda; his two siblings are Hel the death-goddess and Fenrir the wolf. The story of how Thor once nearly caught him on a fishing trip with the giant Hymir, with an ox-head as bait, is one of the strangest in the Prose Edda. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Hymiskvida.

thor-and-jormungandr-nine-paces-from-the.context_blurb: Thor the thunder-god has met the world-serpent Jormungandr twice before their final meeting at Ragnarok, and both times the fight ends without a winner. The first time is at the hall of the giant-king Utgard-Loki, where Thor is challenged to lift a huge grey cat off the floor — but the cat is really the world-serpent in disguise. At Ragnarok the two of them finally face each other in the open on the plain of Vigrid. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

thor-at-utgardaloki-the-horn-the-cat-and.context_blurb: On the first night of his journey east Thor and his companions find what looks like a huge empty hall and crawl inside to sleep. At dawn they realise the 'hall' was actually part of a giant's clothing dropped on the road. The whole trip is one humiliation after another — a drinking-horn he cannot drain, a cat he cannot lift, an old woman he cannot wrestle to the ground. Only at the end does their host Utgard-Loki reveal what each of those contests really was. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

thors-goats-eaten-at-supper-alive-at-daw.context_blurb: In the Norse stories one god does not ride a horse at all. He crosses the sky in a chariot pulled by two goats whose hooves strike sparks against the clouds. At supper on a journey he slaughters and roasts the goats and shares the meat with whichever household he is lodging in — and in the morning he raises them again with his hammer. The bones must all go back onto the hide whole. On one such night a peasant's son cannot resist marrow in a bone — and the goat limps the next morning. Source: Snorri's Gylfaginning.

thors-wedding-veil-recovering-mjolnir-fr.context_blurb: In the Norse poem Thrymskvida, the thunder-god of the Aesir wakes one morning, gropes for the weapon he has always kept beside him, and finds only empty air. He shakes his beard so hard in fury that all Asgard hears it, and calls at once for Loki. Freyja refuses to be married off to the giant Thrym to get the weapon back — so Thor is dressed up as the bride instead, and the wedding feast at the giant's hall is one of the funniest scenes in Norse poetry. Source: Thrymskvida.

tyr-and-garmr-loki-and-heimdallr-the-mut.context_blurb: In the Norse binding of the wolf Fenrir, one god steps forward and lays his hand in the wolf's jaws as a pledge of good faith, and loses it when the trick is sprung. The same god gives his name to the Tuesday of the week in English and most Germanic languages. At Ragnarok he kills and is killed by the hound Garmr; nearby, Loki and Heimdallr are also mutually killed. Sources: Snorri's Gylfaginning; Voluspa.

wiglaf-at-the-dragon-only-one-man-stays.context_blurb: In the Old English poem Beowulf, the hero has grown old. Fifty years after tearing off Grendel's arm in the Danish mead-hall Heorot, Beowulf has been king of the Geats for a long time, ruling in peace. Then trouble comes to his own land — a runaway slave stumbles into a barrow-mound on a headland and steals a golden cup. A dragon that had been sleeping on the hoard for three centuries wakes up and begins burning the countryside. Only one of his twelve chosen companions stays with him at the fight. Source: Beowulf.

the-world-rises-again-lif-and-lifthrasir.context_blurb: In Norse myth Ragnarok is the doom of the gods — Odin swallowed by the wolf, Thor down beside the world-serpent, Surt burning the whole world with fire, and the sea rising to cover every land. But the Voluspa, the great seeress-poem of the Poetic Edda, does not stop there. In stanza 59 the seeress sees something rise again, and names those who come out of a hidden grove to repopulate it — along with golden gaming pieces of the old gods found in the grass of the new fields. Source: Voluspa.

yggdrasil-the-world-tree-and-its-residen.context_blurb: At the centre of the Norse cosmos stands a single enormous tree whose branches spread above all the worlds and whose roots reach down to three separate wells. The Voluspa calls it 'a tall tree, showered with shining loam.' Four stags browse on its leaves, an eagle sits in its top, a dragon gnaws its deepest root, and a squirrel runs insults up and down the trunk between the eagle and the dragon. Source: Grimnismal; Voluspa; Snorri's Gylfaginning.

agatha-of-sicily-the-tongs-and-the-earth.context_blurb:
Agatha, a young Christian of a noble Sicilian family, was killed for her faith around the year 251. Her story, told in the early account of her martyrdom and again in the medieval Golden Legend, made her the beloved patron of her home city, which treasures her veil of white silk to this day and carries it out whenever the volcano above threatens.

Her city was Catania, on Sicily's east coast at the foot of Mount Etna. Agatha lived under the emperor Decius, who demanded that all his subjects sacrifice to Rome's gods on pain of death; it was the first persecution of Christians to reach across the whole empire.

The governor of Sicily, Quintianus, coveted her family's fortune and wanted her as his wife. Agatha refused him and refused to give up her faith, and that made him the villain of her story. He tried first to break her by shame. He handed her over to Aphrodisia, a woman whose name recalls the goddess Aphrodite and who kept a house of ill repute with her nine daughters, and for a month they worked on her and failed.

When Agatha still would not yield, Quintianus had her tortured and her breasts cut off. That night, as she lay in agony in her cell, an old man came to the door with a boy carrying a lamp to light the way. The visitor would not leave until her wounds were healed, and then he named himself: Peter, the apostle. When the jailers opened the cell in the morning, she was whole again.

Catania keeps her feast every 5 February. That morning the bakers set out little round cakes called minni di Sant'Agata, iced snow-white and crowned with a candied cherry, each one filled with sweetened ricotta, the same soft cheese that fills cannoli.

Her veil became the city's shield against the volcano. In the winter of 1886, a tongue of lava from Etna crept toward Nicolosi, a village high on the volcano's southern slope. Catania's archbishop walked out with Agatha's veil and held it up before the flow, and the people of Nicolosi say the lava stopped just short of their walls.

agnes-of-rome-thirteen-years-old-on-the-.context_blurb:
Agnes was a Roman Christian girl of just twelve or thirteen at the start of the fourth century. She was rich and beautiful, and noblemen lined up to marry her, but she had promised her life to Christ and turned every one of them away. Ambrose of Milan wrote the earliest full account of her death around 377.

One of the suitors she refused took his revenge. During the emperor Diocletian's persecution, he went to the Roman officials and named her as a Christian, a crime that could cost her life.

The prefect Sempronius tried to break her with shame. He had her dragged through the streets to a brothel, but the legend says her hair grew long enough to cover her, and any man who came near her was struck blind.

Brought back to court, Agnes was condemned. One version says the soldiers tried to burn her and the fire would not touch her, so an officer took up a sword. In the account Ambrose gives in his book On Virgins, it was the executioner who shook, trembling as though he were the condemned one, while the girl stood calm before him.

Her family laid her in a catacomb beside the Via Nomentana, a road leading out of Rome. Eight days later, the story goes, her grieving parents kept watch at the tomb and saw their daughter there, radiant, surrounded by a flock of white lambs. From that vision came a second feast in her honour, Agnes-secundo, kept in late January until the Roman calendar was revised in the 1960s.

ambrose-of-milan-acclaimed-bishop-before.context_blurb:
In 374 the church of Milan, in northern Italy, needed a new bishop, and rival factions packed the cathedral to fight over the choice. Ambrose, a Roman lawyer and the imperial governor of the province, came only to keep order. He was no priest; he had not even been baptised. His secretary Paulinus later wrote down what happened next.

Ambrose was in the middle of urging both sides to stay calm when a child's voice rang out, "Ambrose for bishop!" Within moments the entire church was chanting it.

Horrified, Ambrose slipped out of the city by night and rode to a friend's country house, hoping to hide until the crowd forgot him. But when the friend learned why he had come, he refused to shelter him and handed him back.

What finally made Ambrose yield was word from the emperor Valentinian, who welcomed the crowd's choice of his own governor. Ambrose was baptised, ordained and made bishop, and he grew into one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Western Church.

anthony-of-the-desert-the-demons-and-pau.context_blurb:
Anthony was an Egyptian Christian of the third century who gave up a fortune for a solitary life in the desert and lived past the age of a hundred. His life story, written around 360 by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, became the pattern for Christian monks in East and West, and Jerome later added a strange tale from his old age.

Anthony grew up in a Nile village and was left rich when his parents died. One Sunday in church he heard the gospel line telling a rich young man to sell all he owned and give it away, and he took the words as spoken to him. Within days he had sold the family land, handed out the money, and gone out into the Egyptian desert for good.

The Greek word for what he chose gave the whole movement its name: monos means alone, a monachos is one who lives alone, and from those words come monk and monasticism. Anthony's first refuge was an empty tomb cut into the cliffs. The story says demons attacked him there and beat him senseless. A friend bringing bread found him lying as if dead, but when Anthony came round he had himself carried back and shouted at the demons that he would not run from their blows.

Crowds of visitors kept finding him, so he went deeper, to a deserted Roman fortress on the Nile. He walled up the door and stayed inside for twenty years while friends passed bread in to him, and when pilgrims finally broke the door down, expecting a living skeleton, they found him healthy and unchanged.

In his old age Anthony learned of a hermit even older than himself, Paul of Thebes, and set out across the wilderness to find him. Jerome's Life of Paul says a creature from Greek myth met him on the way: a centaur, half man and half horse, which grunted, pointed out the road with its right hand and vanished. When Anthony reached Paul's cave, the two old men sat down to talk. A raven had brought Paul half a loaf every day for sixty years, and on the day Anthony came it brought a whole loaf, one half for each old man. Soon afterwards Paul died. Anthony had no spade and was too old to dig, but two lions came out of the desert, whimpered over the body, and pawed out a grave just big enough for a man.

In all his long life in the desert Anthony went to the city only twice, and both times to Alexandria: around 311 to stand by Christians in prison, and around 338 to support his friend Athanasius, the city's bishop. He died in a desert cave, and his last wish was that his disciples bury him where no one could find him and never tell anyone the spot, because he did not want his body turned into a relic to be worshipped. His grave stayed unknown for centuries.

Yet his name travelled anyway. In medieval Europe the Hospitallers of Saint Anthony, monks named after him, ran hospitals for victims of ergotism, a disease from mouldy rye bread that burned in the limbs and turned them black, and people came to call the sickness Saint Anthony's Fire.

augustines-garden-tolle-lege.context_blurb:
Augustine was a brilliant young teacher of public speaking from Roman North Africa who became one of the giants of Christian thought. In his Confessions, often called the first autobiography in Western writing, he tells how his restless life turned around in a Milan garden in 386.

In the 380s Augustine, a young man from Thagaste in what is now Algeria, was teaching rhetoric in Milan. On Sundays he went to hear the city's famous bishop preach; he loved the sermons, but he could not make himself live by them. His mother, Monica, a Christian, had followed him from Africa across the sea to Italy and never stopped praying that he would be baptised, and today Christians honour her as patron of mothers.

Augustine admits that as a teenager he used to pray for purity with an escape clause: he asked God to make him chaste and self-controlled, but not yet, because he was afraid the prayer might be answered too soon. By the late summer of 386 the struggle had become unbearable. During a tense talk with his friend Alypius, Augustine fled down the garden, flung himself on the ground beneath a fig tree and sobbed, asking why it always had to be tomorrow and why not now.

Then, from a house next door, a child's voice began to chant tolle, lege in a singsong, again and again; he could not tell whether a boy or a girl was singing. The words are Latin for take up and read. Augustine took it as a command from God. He went back to where Alypius sat, picked up the book of Paul's letters lying there, and opened it at random.

The verse his eye landed on, from Romans, first warns against wild revelling and drunkenness, then pivots on a single but and commands the reader to put on Jesus Christ, like a garment, and stop making room for the cravings of the flesh. Alypius asked to see the book, read the line that follows, about welcoming one who is weak in the faith, took it as meant for himself, and made the same decision as his friend. Earlier that very day a visitor named Ponticianus had told the two friends the story of Anthony of the Desert.

At the Easter Vigil of 387, on the night of 24 to 25 April, Ambrose, the famous bishop of Milan whose sermons had drawn Augustine for years, baptised him in the cathedral. Alypius was baptised with him, and so was Augustine's teenage son, Adeodatus, whose name means gift of God; the boy had been born years before to a woman Augustine never married.

Augustine sailed home to Africa, took charge of the church in the little harbour town of Hippo Regius, and wrote books that shaped the next thousand years. Pagans were blaming the Christians when Rome was sacked in 410, and Augustine answered them in The City of God, which sets an earthly city built on love of self against a heavenly city built on love of God.

benedict-of-nursia-the-raven-the-cup-and.context_blurb:
Western monks look back to Benedict of Nursia as their father. Born in Norcia in central Italy in the late 400s, he walked away from his studies, lived as a hermit, and finally wrote a Rule for monks, built on prayer and work, that shaped abbeys across Europe for more than a thousand years. Pope Gregory the Great told his life in the Dialogues.

Benedict was a young nobleman whose family sent him to study in Rome, but the city disgusted him, so he left it and made his home as a hermit in a mountain cave at Subiaco, east of the city.

A nearby community of monks begged the holy hermit to be their abbot, but his rule was too strict for them, and they poisoned his wine at supper. Gregory says that when Benedict made the sign of the cross over the cup before drinking, it shattered on the table. He rose calmly, told the monks they had shown what they thought of him, and went back to his cave. Gregory tells of a second poisoning too, when a raven that Benedict fed each day carried a poisoned loaf away at his command.

Followers gathered, and in the Subiaco valley Benedict built twelve small monasteries with twelve monks in each, matching the number of the apostles. Around 529 he led his monks south to Monte Cassino, a mountain halfway between Rome and Naples. A temple of Apollo still stood on its summit; Benedict tore it down and built chapels to John the Baptist and Martin of Tours in its place.

Benedict had a twin sister, Scholastica, who led a community of women near Monte Cassino, and the two met just once a year, in a house midway between their communities, to talk about God. At their last meeting she begged him to stay and talk through the night. He refused, because his Rule forbade it, so she prayed, and a storm broke so fierce that he could not leave. Three days later she died, and from his cell Benedict saw her soul rise to heaven as a dove. Brother and sister lie in one tomb at Monte Cassino.

blandina-at-lyon-the-slave-girl-and-the-.context_blurb:
In 177 AD a mob in Lugdunum, the Roman city we call Lyon in Gaul, turned on the local Christians, and the authorities dragged them into the amphitheatre at the summer games. A letter the surviving churches sent abroad, later copied into the Church History of Eusebius, records their deaths, and the hero of that letter is a slave girl.

Her name was Blandina. Her own Christian mistress, arrested with her, feared the girl was too frail to hold out, but the torturers took turns on her from dawn until dark and at last admitted they were exhausted and had nothing left to try. To every question they put, she gave the same answer: she was a Christian, and her people did nothing to be ashamed of.

Blandina was hung on a post in the arena as food for the beasts, but the animals would not touch her, so the officials returned her to her cell and kept her for the final day of the spectacle. Then she was brought out with Ponticus, a boy of fifteen, and she urged him on until he died.

Then it was her turn. After the whips, she was strapped into an iron chair heated red-hot before the crowd. Next they rolled her in a net and drove a wild steer at her, and it flung her into the air with its horns time after time. Still she did not die, and in the end a gladiator killed her with a dagger.

The Roman officials then had every martyr's body burned and tipped the ashes into the Rhone, so that the current would carry them off and not one relic would be left on earth.

Among the first to die had been the bishop of Lyon, Pothinus, a man over ninety. When the governor demanded to know who the god of the Christians was, the old man answered that if the governor were worthy, he would know. He was beaten so savagely that he died in prison two days later.

brigid-of-kildare-the-flame-the-butter-a.context_blurb:
Brigid of Kildare, an abbess of about the year 500, ranks among the best-loved saints of Ireland. Her Lives, beginning with the one the monk Cogitosus wrote, are full of a generosity that drove her family wild, and of miracles of food, fire and land. She shares her name, her feast and her flame with a far older Irish goddess.

Brigid was the daughter of a Leinster chieftain, Dubthach, and as a girl she handed her father's cattle, cloaks and food to every beggar at the door, until at last he let her become a nun; in time she became a founder of monasteries, remembered as Brigid of Kildare. Around 480 she built her abbey beside a great oak at a place called Cill Dara, the church of the oak, which in English is Kildare, and she took her byname from it.

Her name is older than she is. It belonged to a goddess of fire, of poetry, of healing and of the forge, whom Irish myth makes a daughter of the Dagda, the great father-god of the Tuatha De. Her feast, 1 February, fell on a day already sacred: Imbolc, the old Gaelic first day of spring, when the lambing began and the ewes came into milk.

As a girl, the story goes, Brigid gave the family's whole crock of butter to a poor man. Her mother came home furious, but when they lifted the lid the crock was full again, fuller than before. That miracle made her the patron of dairy work and milkmaids. When the king of the province refused her land for her convent, she asked only for as much ground as her cloak would cover; she spread it out, it stretched across acres of his plain, and Kildare stands there still, in the eastern province of Leinster.

A fire burned at Kildare day and night in her honour. When Gerald of Wales passed through in the 12th century, he found nineteen nuns tending it, one each night in turn, and on the twentieth night, they said, Brigid herself kept the flame.

Kildare was a rare thing, a double monastery, with nuns and monks in separate houses under one abbess. Brigid ruled it alongside Conleth, a metalworker and hermit whom she brought down out of his solitude and made Kildare's first bishop, and the two are said to lie buried together in the old cathedral. Ireland counts three patron saints, and Brigid stands with Patrick, who first carried Christianity to Ireland, and Columba, who built his famous monastery on the Scottish island of Iona.

cecilia-of-rome-three-strokes-and-the-si.context_blurb:
Cecilia is one of the great martyr legends of Rome: a young noblewoman of the third century, married against her will, who died slowly in her own house, which became the church of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere. The legend says that while the instruments played at her wedding she sang to God in her heart, and so she later became the patron saint of music.

Cecilia, forced by her family to wed a pagan nobleman, won him over to her faith on their wedding night. She told her husband, Valerian, that an angel guarded her virginity and that he would see it too if he were baptised. Valerian went to Pope Urban at the third milestone on the Appian Way, was baptised, came home and saw the angel.

Then Valerian brought his own brother, Tiburtius, to be baptised at the same milestone, and the two brothers died for their faith before Cecilia did. The prefect Almachius then condemned Cecilia herself. Three times the executioner struck at her neck and still could not cut off her head, and she lived on for three days, teaching the Christians who crowded around her bed, giving her goods to the poor and begging the pope to make her house a church.

In the 14th century Geoffrey Chaucer put her story into the Canterbury Tales, giving it to a pilgrim known only by her office, the Second Nun, who draws on the Golden Legend and explains the name Cecilia, fancifully, as lily of heaven.

christopher-the-giant-at-the-river-and-t.context_blurb:
Christopher is the giant saint of medieval legend. The Golden Legend, the great medieval book of saints' lives by Jacobus de Voragine, tells how a huge man searching for the mightiest lord on earth ended up carrying a child across a river, and how that crossing gave him his name.

His Greek name, Christophoros, joins Christos, Christ, to the verb for carrying: Christopher means Christ-bearer.

Before his baptism the Golden Legend calls him Reprobus, from a Latin word meaning rejected. He was a heathen giant from the land of Canaan, twelve cubits tall, about eighteen feet, a size deliberately past any real man.

Reprobus wanted to serve the strongest master alive. He served a mighty king until he saw the king flinch at the mention of the devil, and then he left to serve the devil, the master even a king feared. But the devil in his turn flinched at another name, Christ's, and so the giant set off again to find the master the devil feared.

He became a ferryman, carrying travellers on his shoulders across a dangerous river. One stormy night a small child begged a crossing, and the boy weighed more with every step, until the water nearly closed over the giant's head. On the far bank Reprobus gasped that the whole world could not have weighed more. The child answered that he had carried more than the world: he had carried the one who made it. In the legend, the child was Christ. To prove it, he had the giant drive his walking staff into the ground, and by morning the dead wood had sprouted leaves, flowers and dates, like the rod of Aaron that blossomed in the Bible.

Some Eastern icons give Christopher the head of a dog. Scholars trace the image to a scribe who garbled the Latin Cananeus, Canaanite, into canineus, dog-like, and from that slip grew a tale that he came from a race of dog-headed men.

columba-of-iona-the-psalter-the-battle-a.context_blurb:
Columba was an Irish monk born to royalty, descended from Niall of the Nine Hostages, who in 563 sailed to Scotland and founded the island monastery of Iona. His biographer Adomnan tells of a quarrel over a book, a terrible battle, an exile and a beast in the River Ness.

In Irish he was Colum Cille, the dove of the church, which later became the Latin Columba.

Around 560 the young Columba spent nights secretly copying a beautiful psalter belonging to his old teacher Finnian at Movilla. Finnian claimed the copy too, and High King Diarmait judged for him with a line later called the first copyright ruling: as every calf belongs to its cow, so every copy belongs to its book.

The quarrel ended in blood. In 561 the clans of the O Neill fought the High King's army at Cul Dreimhne near Drumcliff, and about three thousand men died, a slaughter that tradition blamed on Columba. A synod of Irish abbots set his penance: exile, until he had won for the faith as many souls as had died in the battle. In 563 Columba and twelve companions, as many as the apostles, crossed from Derry in a curragh, a boat of hides, to the coast of Scotland, and a royal kinsman there gave him the little island of Iona.

In 565, Adomnan says, Columba was at the River Ness in the land of the Picts when his companion Lugne swam across and a monster surged up out of the river toward him. Lifting his hand in the sign of the cross, the saint commanded the creature to go no further and not touch the man, but to go back at once, and it fled as though hauled away by ropes. It is the first Loch Ness monster story, though it happened on the river.

In 597 the old abbot sat in his cell copying the Psalms. He reached the verse promising that those who seek God will lack no good thing, laid down his pen and said that he must stop there and that another must write the rest; that other was his cousin Baithene, who became the second abbot of Iona. Columba walked to the church and died before the altar.

For two centuries after his death Iona's monks were among the finest scribes in the Atlantic world, and around 800 they began the Book of Kells, the most richly painted gospel book of the early Middle Ages; Viking raids later forced the monks to flee Iona, carrying the book with them, and it is now in Trinity College Dublin.

genevieve-of-paris-prayer-against-attila.context_blurb: Genevieve is born around the year 420 in a village a few miles west of the Roman town of Lutetia — the old Latin name for the city that would become one of the great capitals of Europe and whose patron saint she still is. In 451, when the Hunnic armies swept across Gaul, she called the city's women to prayer rather than flight, and the Huns swerved past. Decades later, when a different conquering army did arrive, she negotiated with its king. Her burial-place later became a famous Roman-style domed monument in the Latin Quarter. Source: Vita Genovefae.

george-and-the-dragon-of-silene.context_blurb: The historical George whom the medieval world made into its most famous dragon-slaying knight was in real life a Christian soldier of the Roman army, executed on 23 April 303 CE at Lydda in Palestine. His dragon-fight is a later story, added by the Golden Legend of Jacobus de Voragine in the thirteenth century — a Libyan city threatened by a dragon in its lake, a princess sent out as a sacrifice, and a knight who tames the dragon with a girdle. George became the patron saint of England by vow of King Edward III. Source: Jacobus de Voragine, Legenda Aurea.

ignatius-of-antioch-the-wheat-of-god.context_blurb: Around 108 CE a Christian bishop was arrested in the Syrian capital under the emperor Trajan and sentenced to be sent to the arena in Rome. He spent the last months of his life walking under guard across Anatolia to his execution, writing seven letters to the churches along the way (and one to Bishop Polycarp of Smyrna) that are among the earliest surviving Christian writings outside the New Testament. His chain-gang of ten Roman soldiers he nicknamed 'leopards.' Source: Letters of Ignatius; Eusebius.

jerome-the-lion-and-the-vulgate.context_blurb: In a cave-cell in Bethlehem, an old scholar named Jerome bent over his lamp-lit desk for the last thirty-four years of his life, working on one enormous project at the request of Pope Damasus: a single Latin Bible for all of Western Europe. He had learned Hebrew from Jewish teachers in Palestine so he could translate the Old Testament straight from the original. The medieval legend adds a lion who turned up at his monastery with a thorn in its paw and became his companion. Source: Jerome's letters; Golden Legend.

lawrence-of-rome-the-gridiron-and-the-tr.context_blurb: In 258 CE, during the brief but severe persecution under the Roman emperor Valerian, Pope Sixtus II was arrested and executed. Three days later the same emperor's officials came for the pope's chief deacon in Rome, who held the role of archdeacon and was in charge of the Roman church's silver plate, its register of help to the widows and poor, and all of its daily charity. He was ordered to hand over the church's treasure. The way he answered that order became one of the most famous moments of early Christian defiance. Source: Prudentius, Peristephanon 2.

martin-of-tours-half-a-cloak-at-the-gate.context_blurb: One bitter winter night on the road into a city in northern Gaul, a young Roman cavalry officer named Martin — a native of Pannonia on the Danube — came upon a beggar shivering nearly naked in the freezing wind. He had no money and nothing to give, so he drew his sword, cut his own cloak in half, and handed one piece to the beggar. That night he dreamed of Christ wearing the half-cloak. The rest of his life — his refusal to fight before the battle of Worms, the founding of his monastery at Marmoutier, his bishopric of Tours — is told in Sulpicius Severus's Vita Martini. Source: Sulpicius Severus, Vita Martini.

nicholas-of-myra-three-bags-through-the-.context_blurb: Nicholas was a fourth-century bishop of Myra in Asia Minor who became the most beloved popular saint of the Christian world. One of his most famous legends tells how, when he learned of three sisters whose impoverished father could not afford dowries and was about to sell them, he threw three bags of gold through their window at night to save them. In the medieval Netherlands and across northern Europe his December feast grew into a long tradition that eventually gave the modern world Santa Claus. Source: Vita Nicolai; Dutch folklore.

patrick-of-ireland-six-years-a-shepherd-.context_blurb: The patron saint of Ireland, whose feast fills the streets of Dublin, Boston, and New York every 17 March, was born around 385 CE into a Roman-Christian family in Roman Britain. His father Calpurnius was a local Roman magistrate and his grandfather had been a priest. At about sixteen he was kidnapped by Irish raiders and spent six years as a shepherd-slave in Ireland before escaping. Years later he came back as a bishop. His own words in his Confessio open with a famous one-line self-description. Source: Patrick, Confessio.

perpetua-and-felicity-the-ladder-and-the.context_blurb: In the year 203 CE, during the persecution under the emperor Septimius Severus, a young noblewoman named Perpetua of Carthage was arrested with a group of fellow catechumens including an eight-months-pregnant enslaved woman named Felicity. Perpetua kept a diary in prison that survives — one of the earliest first-person documents by a Christian woman. The whole party was finally brought into the arena, which the two women faced side by side on the day of the games. Source: Passio Perpetuae et Felicitatis.

polycarp-of-smyrna-eighty-and-six-years.context_blurb: A very old Christian bishop was dragged out of a farmhouse outside Smyrna on the west coast of Asia Minor, an elderly disciple of the apostle John from the generation before. He was brought back to the city to face the Roman proconsul in the stadium. In the surviving letter of his church to the other Asian churches, his last words to the proconsul are preserved — a famous answer when he was asked to curse Christ. He is one of the earliest named martyrs after the apostles themselves. Source: Martyrdom of Polycarp.

sebastian-the-arrows-the-widow-and-the-c.context_blurb: A young officer in the emperor Diocletian's Praetorian Guard has been secretly visiting fellow soldiers in the cells to encourage them; he himself is a secret Christian, and he is denounced. Diocletian orders him executed. The famous image of his death — a young man tied to a post full of arrows — turns out, in the Legenda Aurea, not to be the end at all; a Roman widow named Lucina found him still alive and nursed him back to health. He was later martyred a second time. Source: Legenda Aurea.

simeon-stylites-thirty-seven-years-on-a-.context_blurb: A Syrian shepherd boy joined a monastery near Antioch in the fourth century, but his fasts and self-denial were so extreme that the other monks asked him to leave. He moved out to a stone hut alone — and then, trying to escape the crowds who still followed him, climbed up on top of a stone pillar and lived there for the rest of his life, raising the pillar higher as he went. The pillar's ruins at Qalat Simaan in Syria were a famous Christian pilgrimage site for centuries. Source: Theodoret of Cyrrhus, Religious History.

bede-the-venerable-at-jarrow-the-church-.context_blurb:
Bede was an English monk of the double monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow in Northumbria, in the far north of England, and later ages called him the Venerable Bede. He wrote the first great history of the English church, and the story of how Christianity came to the English is still told mostly in his words.

Around 731 he finished his masterpiece in five books, the Historia Ecclesiastica, still the most important source for Anglo-Saxon England. He dedicated it to Ceolwulf, king of Northumbria, who had seen an early draft and sent back comments.

One of Bede's stories is about Caedmon, an unlettered herdsman who looked after the cattle of Whitby Abbey. When the harp went round at feasts he slipped away, ashamed that he could not sing, until one night in the cowshed a stranger in a dream told him to sing, and he woke able to make songs about God in English. His short hymn of nine lines is the oldest Old English poem on record.

Bede also tells why Rome sent missionaries to the English at all. Pope Gregory the Great, walking through the slave market in Rome, saw fair-haired boys from Britain for sale, learned that their people were called Angles, and made his famous pun: they were not Angles but angels. In 597 Gregory sent the monk Augustine to Canterbury to preach to them.

Bede even fixed the way the West counts its years. A monk named Dionysius Exiguus, Denis the Little, had worked out the Anno Domini count from the birth of Jesus in 525 while drawing up a table of Easter dates. Bede adopted it throughout his History and in his treatise on time, and that made it the West's standard.

Bede died at Jarrow, but in the 11th century his bones were moved to Durham Cathedral, where they lie in the Galilee Chapel under a Latin verse naming Bede the Venerable. In 1899 Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church, the only native of Britain to hold that title.

In the spring of 735, the night before Ascension Day, the old monk was dying but would not stop working: he was dictating an English translation of the Gospel of John for his own people, and his disciple Cuthbert wrote down what followed. That evening the boy scribe Wilberht told him that one sentence was still unwritten. Scribe cito, Bede answered, telling the boy to write it quickly. When Wilberht said it was finished, Bede agreed that it was finished, and he died on the floor of his cell singing Glory be to the Father.

bernard-of-clairvaux-and-the-second-crus.context_blurb:
Bernard of Clairvaux was a French monk of the 12th century and one of the most powerful voices of the Middle Ages: a mystic, a writer of sermons, an adviser to popes and kings, and the preacher who launched the Second Crusade.

In 1113 Bernard, a 22-year-old nobleman from Burgundy, arrived at Citeaux, a struggling new abbey close to dying out, bringing some thirty kinsmen and friends he had persuaded to become monks with him, and their arrival saved the house that became the mother of the whole Cistercian order.

Three years later Abbot Stephen Harding sent him to found a daughter house in a wild place on the river Aube known as the Valley of Wormwood. Bernard renamed it Clairvaux, the bright valley, ruled it as abbot for the rest of his life, and became known by its name. There he spent eighteen years preaching his way through the Song of Songs, the Bible's love poem, and he had reached his 86th sermon, still unfinished, when he died in 1153.

Then came news from the East. On Christmas Eve 1144 the warlord Zengi captured Edessa, the northernmost of the four crusader states and the first of them to fall to Muslim rule, and Pope Eugenius III proclaimed a Second Crusade to win it back, asking Bernard to preach it.

At Vezelay, on Easter Sunday of 1146, Bernard preached to a crowd so vast that it had to gather on the hillside outside the basilica, with King Louis VII and Queen Eleanor of Aquitaine among them. Volunteers surged forward to take the cross, and when no cloth crosses were left, Bernard tore his own white monk's habit into strips to make more.

The crusade he preached ended in disaster. The French and German armies of Louis VII and Conrad III reached the East, but their great attack on Damascus fell apart after a siege of only four days in July 1148, and the expedition broke up. Bernard wrote afterwards that God had not shown him why it failed.

boniface-felling-the-donar-oak-at-fritzl.context_blurb:
Winfrid, a monk from Devon in England, crossed the Rhine early in the 700s to preach to the tribes of the German forests, who still worshipped the old gods. He grew into the Germans' great missionary bishop, and his most famous moment came with an axe in his hands.

In 719 Pope Gregory II renamed him in Latin as Boniface, meaning roughly one who does good, and sent him back as a missionary bishop for Germania.

In 723, at Geismar near Fritzlar in Hesse, Boniface took an axe to a great oak sacred to Donar, the thunder god the Norse called Thor, while a crowd of pagans watched, sure their god would strike him dead. Willibald, who wrote Boniface's life, says he had made only a few cuts when a great wind blew up, and the giant tree came down and broke apart into four trunks of equal length. No lightning fell, and the crowd that had been cursing him began to bless him instead. From the timber of the fallen tree Boniface built a little wooden chapel on the very spot and dedicated it to Saint Peter, binding his mission to Rome and to the pope who had sent him.

Boniface never stopped travelling. As an old man he went back to Frisia, on the North Sea coast of today's Netherlands, and on 5 June 754, as he stood waiting at the river Borne near Dokkum to confirm new converts, a band of armed pagans fell on him and some fifty companions and killed them. The raiders broke open the missionaries' chests expecting treasure and found only books.

Tradition says Boniface raised a book over his head as a shield, and the killing stroke cut straight through it. Fulda Cathedral treasures a battered manuscript, the Ragyndrudis Codex, slashed deep through cover and pages, as that very book, though it is a collection of Latin writings rather than a gospel.

catherine-of-siena-writing-to-popes.context_blurb:
Catherine of Siena was born in 1347 in the Italian hill town of Siena, the daughter of Lapa and of Jacopo Benincasa, a wool-dyer. She had no rank and no army, yet she grew into one of the most powerful mystics and political voices of 14th-century Europe, a woman who wrote letters to popes and told them what to do.

Catherine was born a twin near the end of an enormous family: her parents had twenty-five children in all, and her twin sister died as a baby. At about six, walking home with her brother, she stopped dead in the street and stared at the sky above the church of San Domenico; she said later that she had seen Christ there, dressed in a pope's robes, blessing her.

She vowed her life to God while still a small girl. When her family tried to marry her off to the widower of her elder sister, she cut her long hair off to make herself an unfit bride. Her family gave in at last and let her wear the Dominican habit.

In June 1376 she made her boldest journey, to Avignon, the city on the Rhone where the popes had lived since 1309, close under the power of the kings of France. She faced Pope Gregory XI in person and urged him to take his court back to Rome. On 17 January 1377 he rode into Rome again.

charlemagne-and-alcuin-at-aachen-the-pal.context_blurb:
Charlemagne, king of the Franks, ruled most of western Europe around the year 800. He was a warrior, but he also gathered the best scholars he could find to his palace at Aachen, and his friend and biographer Einhard left a vivid picture of the man and his court.

On Christmas Day in the year 800, while Charlemagne knelt at Mass in Saint Peter's in Rome, Pope Leo III stepped behind him, crowned him and proclaimed him Emperor of the Romans. Einhard says Charlemagne later claimed he would never have gone into the church that day had he known.

Charlemagne found his chief scholar at Parma in 781: Alcuin, a deacon from England heading home from Rome, whom all Europe already reckoned the most learned man alive. Alcuin had been schooled in the great library of York, in Northumbria, and Charlemagne talked him into running the palace school. At Aachen Charlemagne raised a stone chapel modelled on a church he had admired in Italy, San Vitale at Ravenna, and he even shipped marble columns north from Ravenna to build it. It still stands today.

The scholars of the palace school gave each other playful nicknames from the classics and the Bible: Alcuin was Albinus, the poet Angilbert was Homer, and Charlemagne himself was David, the warrior-king of Israel. Einhard shares a touching secret: the emperor kept wax tablets under his pillow so he could practise forming letters whenever he woke in the night, but he never learned to write well, though he could read and dictated fluently.

Alcuin's monasteries spread a new handwriting, a clear, rounded small hand with gaps left between words, so that scribes across the empire could copy the Bible without errors. Six centuries later Italian humanists found these books in old libraries and copied the letters eagerly, believing they had found actual ancient Roman writing; from their copies comes the lowercase type you are reading now.

After his death in 814, Charlemagne was laid to rest in his Aachen chapel. In its upper gallery stands a plain throne of marble slabs taken from ancient Roman buildings and clamped with bronze, and German kings were crowned on it for six hundred years, from Otto I in 936 to Ferdinand I in 1531.

clare-of-assisi-running-to-francis-in-th.context_blurb:
Clare was a young noblewoman of Assisi, a hill town in central Italy, who, in the early 1200s, ran away from her family to follow Francis, the barefoot preacher who had given up everything. Her community of sisters, the Poor Clares, became the women's branch of the Franciscan movement.

Clare grew up in her noble family's palazzo beside the cathedral of San Rufino, and from an upstairs window she could hear Francis, a dozen years her senior, preaching to crowds in the square below.

In 1212, on Palm Sunday night, eighteen-year-old Clare refused the wealthy husband her family had chosen and fled in the dark, down across the fields to the Portiuncula, the tiny chapel below the town where Francis lived with his brothers, who met her with torches. She left by a narrow side door that Assisi's great houses kept for one purpose only, carrying out the dead for burial, which is why it was called the door of the dead. At the chapel she left her old life behind on the spot. Francis took her vows, clothed her in coarse cloth like his brothers', and sheared off her long hair.

Her family soon found her. Her uncle and armed kinsmen came to the convent where Francis had hidden her, meaning to drag her home and marry her off, but Clare gripped the altar cloth and pulled back her veil to show her cropped head. A shorn head marked a woman given to God, and her family could no longer marry her off. Days later her sister Agnes joined her.

In September 1240 the emperor Frederick II's hired Saracen soldiers stormed toward Assisi, right up to the walls of her convent. Clare, too ill to stand, had her sisters carry her out and place in her hands the consecrated host, the bread of the Mass, in its covered vessel from the chapel, and when she lifted it up before them, the soldiers withdrew. She died in 1253.

teaches.46eb4ef8ac: Clare, too ill to stand, had her sisters carry her out and place in her hands the consecrated host, the bread of the Mass, in its covered vessel from the chapel, and when she lifted it up before them, the soldiers withdrew.

cuthbert-of-lindisfarne-and-the-otters-w.context_blurb:
Cuthbert is the best-loved saint of northern England: a shepherd boy who became a monk and a hermit and lived out his life around Lindisfarne, the tidal island off the coast of Northumbria. Bede wrote his life, full of wonders, among them the otters that came out of the sea to warm his feet after a night of prayer in the cold waves.

In 651, while keeping sheep on the Northumbrian hills, the boy Cuthbert saw angels in the night sky bearing a soul into heaven, and in the morning he learned that Aidan of Lindisfarne, the Irish monk from Iona who had founded Lindisfarne, had died at that very hour. The boy decided to become a monk.

Bede tells how the young monk once spent a whole night praying waist-deep in the freezing sea, and how at dawn two otters came out of the waves, warmed his feet with their breath and dried them with their fur. Even a tidal monastery was not quiet enough for him. In 676 he withdrew to Inner Farne, a bare rock out in the North Sea, where he dug a well, grew barley and built the walls of his cell so high that he could see nothing but the sky.

Cuthbert was buried on Lindisfarne. Eleven years later, in 698, the monks opened his coffin to move his bones into a shrine and found his body whole and uncorrupted, his robes still fresh, the most famous wonder ever told of him.

When Viking raids struck Lindisfarne from 793, the monks fled with his coffin and bore it from place to place across northern England for more than a century. They rested many years at Chester-le-Street, and around 995 they settled at last at Durham, where the great cathedral, begun in 1093, was built over his tomb.

cyril-and-methodius-the-slavic-alphabet.context_blurb:
Cyril and Methodius were two Greek brothers from the Byzantine port of Thessalonica, a city where Slavic could be heard in every street. In the ninth century they became missionaries to the Slavs, and they were the first to write the Slavic language down.

Methodius was the elder. The younger, born Constantine, took the monastic name Cyril late in life, in Rome, and that is the name by which both brothers are remembered.

Around 863 Cyril set off for Moravia, found that the Slavs had no letters of their own, and designed an alphabet fitted to the sounds of their speech. Historians call it Glagolitic, from glagol, the Slavic for word. The alphabet called Cyrillic, which honours his name, was built after his death by his students, mostly out of Greek capital letters.

In 867, passing through Venice, Cyril had to defend his right to hold services in Slavic. His opponents said that God could be praised only in the three tongues of the sign Pilate had set over the cross, Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and the Slavonic sources call their view the Pilatian heresy.
